#4515. Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders

Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the company’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.

That’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.

Napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter. He said that at the start of Q3, the company had orders where it “would take sometimes two weeks to deliver to the customer, and so we would lose the order.”

He said Lucid now has visibility on which cars are being built, where they’re shipped, where they’re stored, and when they can reach a customer. A new commercial team also now sells the cars it knows are available on the day a customer wants one.

Lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered in the first half of 2026, including 5,500 built but only 3,093 delivered in Q1. Its inventory hit $1.38 billion on the balance sheet at the end of June, which is why we reported earlier this year that Lucid had to adjust production after a bloated Q1 inventory.

So Lucid had thousands of cars on lots and in transit, and it was still losing buyers because it couldn’t match a car to an order fast enough.

In Q3, Lucid cut production to 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806, down 7% year over year. Finished goods inventory fell by almost 15% during the quarter, according to new CFO Alexander De Bock. Inventory stood at $1.22 billion on September 30.

Tesla learned this lesson the hard way during the Model 3 ramp.

By Q3 2018, Tesla was making roughly 4,000 Model 3s per week. That’s more cars every week than Lucid delivers in a full quarter today. Deliveries tripled or quadrupled in some markets, and the bottleneck moved from the factory to the trucks.

Elon Musk tweeted in September 2018 that Tesla had “gone from production hell to delivery logistics hell.” A week later, he said Tesla was facing an “extreme shortage of car carrier trailers” and had started building its own car carriers to keep cars moving. Tesla also launched door-to-door delivery and asked existing owners to help at delivery centers.

It didn’t stop there. In November 2018, with the federal tax credit about to be cut in half for Tesla buyers, Musk said Tesla had bought trucking companies and locked in contracts with major haulers. Tesla moved cars east by truck instead of rail to cut weeks off transit times.

Tesla delivered 83,500 vehicles in Q3 2018, including 55,840 Model 3s, a record at the time.

When Model 3 reached Europe in February 2019, the first ship docked at Zeebrugge in Belgium and Tesla immediately had trouble processing the cars at the port.

About a week after the first ship arrived, Tesla ended its contract with the company preparing Model 3s at the port and took over the work itself. The target was 3,000 cars per week coming through one port.

It worked. By March 2019, Tesla delivered more than 5,300 Model 3s in Norway alone, making it the best-selling car in the country by a wide margin. A car that’s sitting at a port or on a lot doesn’t make anyone money. Tesla treated delivery speed as a sales tool, not a back-office job.

We later learned from Musk himself that this “logistic hell” was almost the nail in Tesla’s coffin. The CEO said that Tesla was at the brink of bankruptcy at the time.

I like to think people were relatively patient with Tesla's growing pains when Model 3 was ramping up in 2018, largely because there weren't many alternatives for a sporty, relatively affordable EV.

But it's 2026. Buyers have plenty of options now, and the patience that early EV adopters once had for these kinds of mistakes is long gone.

This is one of the most embarrassing admissions we’ve heard on an earnings call, and credit to Napoli for saying it out loud. Most executives would have blamed “demand” and moved on.

But it explains a lot. Lucid’s problem has never been the cars. The Air and Gravity are excellent products. The problem has been everything around them: service, software, and now we learn, basic inventory tracking. When you’re spending about $273,000 for every car you deliver, losing a buyer because you can’t find their car two weeks after they ordered is brutal.

Tesla solved this at 4,000 Model 3s a week while fighting for its own survival. Lucid is moving fewer than 300 cars a week. This isn’t a hard problem at that scale. It’s a discipline problem, and Napoli is right to call it that.

The twin-turbo 4.0-liter engine will pair with a hybrid system, and the duo will make nearly 1000 horsepower combined.

There’s a new V-8-powered Lotus on the way, and we’ve just got our first proper look at the powertrain. While the supercar uses the codename Type 135, most of the world expects it to resurrect the British brand’s legendary Espirt nameplate, and now we know that it’ll have a brand-new 4.0-liter V-8. The engine will team up with a dual-clutch automatic transmission, and both will be built by a company called Horse Powertrain.

The twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8, called the Horse W40, will come in a hot-V configuration, meaning it’ll store its turbos between the cylinder banks, rather than on either side of them. Horse says the combustion half of the powertrain will be responsible for generating 670 horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque, though it’ll be part of a larger hybrid system that Lotus promises will combine for at least 986 horsepower. #4513. Ford Recalling 33,000 Explorer Police Interceptors Because of Interior Lights That Might Not Turn Off

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

A software glitch can trigger a phantom “Global On” command, leaving the map lights illuminated even when officers try to turn them off.

Lights on a police car are extremely important. From flashing red and blue emergency lights to spotlights designed to illuminate whatever officers are investigating, they serve a variety of purposes. But sometimes, it's best if there are no lights on at all. That's why Ford Explorer Police Interceptors are equipped with a Police Dark Car feature: the last thing an officer wants during a nighttime stakeout is unwanted interior lighting. Unfortunately, more than 33,000 Explorer Police Interceptors have a problem that can leave their map lights stuck on, and it's led to a safety recall.

According to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, Ford is recalling 33,578 Explorer Police Interceptor vehicles from the 2026 and 2027 model years. The problem involves the overhead console, which can incorrectly interpret an electrical signal during vehicle startup as a command to turn on the map lights. Ford calls this a “phantom ‘Global On’ condition.”

Should this condition occur, not only will the map lights remain illuminated, but they can't be turned off using the individual switches. That can be annoying and distracting while driving, but it can be even more troublesome if the officers inside are trying to keep a low profile. The condition also violates Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) No. 101, Section S5.3.4(a). Under that standard, front-row interior lighting must have a means of being switched off.

Vehicles built between March 3, 2025, and October 23, 2026, are included in the recall. As of October 13, Ford received 69 warranty claims related to the defect. No crashes or injuries have been reported. Ford dealers will replace the overhead consoles in vehicles built before July 9, 2026, while newer vehicles will have their consoles inspected for an updated component. If the correct component is already installed, the console will simply be reinstalled; otherwise, it will be replaced. All repairs will be performed free of charge, as is required by federal law.

Owners are expected to receive notification letters between December 28 and December 30, 2026. In the meantime, police officers planning any nighttime stakeouts might want to use another vehicle until their Explorer has been repaired.

#4512. Critically endangered tortoises slurp up pumpkin soup

Published Nov 12, 2026 2:00 PM EST

‘Tis the season for pumpkin: the “Superbowl of Pumpkin Weigh Offs,” pumpkin spice lattes, and prepping Thanksgiving feasts. One group of endangered tortoises are enjoying the season with a soup served inside a pumpkin bowl.

The trio of critically endangered Asian giant tortoises (Manouria emys phayrei) at the Turtle Survival Center (TSC) in South Carolina recently feasted on this specially made soup with gusto.

“Pumpkin is a great seasonal addition for the turtles,” keeper Carly Sprott tells Popular Science. “It helps keep them hydrated, contains vitamins A and C, as well as fiber that aids in digestion. It is not something we would feed turtles as their entire meal very often, instead we offer balanced meals of fresh salads and various proteins depending on the species’ needs. They were absolutely thrilled when they received a taste of one of their favorite fall snacks!”

In the wild, Asian giant tortoises are found in tropical and subtropical mountainous evergreen forests in parts of Bangladesh and Indonesia. These freshwater turtles are listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List, and their primary threats are habitat destruction, collection for local consumption, and collection for pet and food trades. Freshwater turtles like these help their ecosystems by dispersing seeds after eating local plants, dig burrows that other animals in the area can use as shelter, and maintain some balance in the food chain. They also eat plenty of algae and invasive plants, which then improves water quality.

These particular Asian giant tortoises were the first turtles brought into the rescue center in 2013. They were taken from the wild legally in the 1990s, before there were stricter regulations regarding turtle conservation. While the team at the TSC does not name the hundreds of turtles living there, these three do have names since they were the center’s first turtles. They are named Emy-Sue, Emy-Jane, and Emy-Phay, which comes from the Asian giant tortoises’ scientific name—Manouria emys phayrei.

To make things fun, the team creates seasonal treats like these pumpkin soups. In the summer, they will hollow out watermelons. “They love to eat and always follow us around the enclosure to see if they will be awarded an extra treat,” Sprott says.

When they are not eating soup, they spend their days soaking in fresh water pools, warming underneath heat lamps, and roaming around in their large outdoor space.

The TSC is home to 27 turtle and tortoise species, including some of the world’s most endangered that need help.

“Currently, over half of all turtle species in the world are threatened with extinction. These captivating reptiles need our support,” says Sprott . “A few things the community can do to help include cleaning up litter that washes into waterways, supporting local conservation efforts, and treating wildlife with respect in their natural habitats.”

#4511. Kia launches two new PV5 electric van variants in the UK

Kia opened orders for two new PV5 electric van variants, the PV5 Chassis and PV5 Cargo L2/H2, in the UK.

The PV5 is Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business. Built on Hyundai Motor’s dedicated modular skateboard platform, E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to enable “limitless possibilities.”

So far, the PV5 has mostly been available in Passenger and Cargo body styles with several different variations.

Kia added the PV5 Chassis, an open-bed model that can be converted into just about anything. In the UK, Kia is offering conversions through TGS Automotive Group, including lightweight tipper, Dropside, and Box solutions.

The PV5 Chassis is available exclusively with the long-range 71.2 kWh battery in the UK, which Kia said could offer a potential WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km).

For reference, the PV5 Cargo L2/H1, which uses the same 71.2 kWh battery, offers a WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km). Other markets will also have a standard-range 51.1 kWh option.

The Chassis model is 4,610 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,935 mm tall, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.

Its compact size and 5.5-meter turning radius, Kia said, make it easy to maneuver in city streets, construction sites, and other tight work areas.

Inside, the PV5 Chassis features two seats. Like other variants, it includes a 12.9″ navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The Chassis model supports DC fast charging up to 120 kW, enabling the battery to charge from 10% to 80% in about 30 minutes. Using an 11 kW AC supply, it takes about 6 hours and 30 minutes to charge from 10% to 100%.

Payload depends on the configuration. Kia said the Dropside offers a payload of up to 633 kg, while the Tipper can carry 561 kg.

In the UK, the PV5 Chassis is now on sale from £32,916 ($43,400) on the road, including the expected £5,000 ($6,700) UK Zero Emission Van Grant.

However, it’s an “incomplete vehicle,” as Kia describes it. The converted PV5 Dropside is priced from £40,110 ($53,500) on the road, including the ZEVG, while the PV5 Tipper starts at £41,310 ($55,000).

Kia also launched the larger PV5 Cargo L2/H2 in the UK. The new variant is 4,695mm long, 1,895mm wide, and 2,200mm high, with a 2,995mm wheelbase.

The taller roof opens up an internal cargo-area height of 1,815mm. It also offers a greater load capacity than the L1/H1 and L2/H2, with 5.2 cubic meters.

It’s available in three- and four-door configurations with the choice of two or three seats. The three-door versions have a maximum payload of 630 kg, while the four-door models have dual sliding doors and offer a payload of up to 600 kg. Both versions can tow up to 1,500 kg.

Like the Chassis model, the PV5 Cargo L2/H2 is available in the UK exclusively with the 71.2 kWh battery, which provides a WLTP range of up to 239 miles.

Inside, it features the same setup as the other PV5 variants, including a 12.9″ touchscreen navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display.

The base PV5 Cargo L2/H2 Essential two-seat starts at £35,016 ($46,700), on the road, including ZEVG.

#4510. Lincoln Recalls 37K Navigators for Front Seat That May Move on Its Own

The recall affects 2025–2027 models with the ‘Chauffeur Seat Feature.’ Greasy fingers may play a role.

No one likes greasy fingers, especially when they might cause a power-adjustable seat to move on its own. That’s the issue plaguing nearly 37,000 Lincoln Navigators, which are being recalled because their front passenger seat may unexpectedly move.

The recall involves 2025–2027 Navigator models with the “Chauffeur Seat Feature.” This function allows people sitting in the second row to control the front passenger seat’s movements via a touchscreen that’s built into the center console.

Based on the recall documents that Lincoln submitted to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), residue on the touch-activated display may cause the front passenger seat to unexpectedly move forward or back or recline up or down. Plus, if the home screen button is pressed on the rear touchscreen at the same time as a seat adjustment, Lincoln says this may cause the seat to move all the way to the end of its track without any buttons being pressed again.

See all results for new 2026 Lincoln Navigator for sale near 98837

While an empty seat that moves on its own is mostly just spooky, an occupied one could potentially cause an injury. That’s why Lincoln is asking owners to bring their affected Navigators to an authorized dealer so that the Chauffeur Seat Feature can be deactivated. This will be done for free, but it doesn’t sound like that function will work anymore. Finally, Lincoln says that both dealers and owners should have been notified by mail by now. If you haven’t received a letter and want to know if your SUV is part of the recall, you can use this feature on the NHTSA website to look up your VIN or search by year, make, and model, which will also show any other recall-related alerts.

#4509. Customer busted for using AI image of burnt pizza to scam restaurant

Published Nov 12, 2026 3:03 PM EST

Generative artificial intelligence is driving an unprecedented wave of scams, from vocal clone politician phone calls to uncomfortably realistic deepfake images. While most of these are designed and coordinated by groups of bad actors hoping to cast the widest net possible, some are the work of individuals simply attempting to pull one over on specific targets. Many AI con jobs are more convincing than others, but one pizzeria owner in Los Angeles almost immediately suspected a recent patron’s complaint once they saw the supposed “evidence.”

After receiving their pizza from Masa of Echo Park via DoorDash, a customer named “Dana B” demanded a full refund for what they claimed was an inedible, burnt pie. Accompanying their grammatically questionable message was a picture of what appeared to be a charred Chicago-style pizza.

“its burnt to heck. burnt. black. cant eat it. dont wanna eat cancer…,” they wrote in their complaint.

However, Masa owner Rhonda Reynolds knew almost instantly that the allegation was categorically false.

“It was impossible. It was absolutely impossible,” she told local news outlet KTLA 5.

Reynolds uploaded the photo into an app called “Is This AI,” which offered a 96 percent certainty that the picture was faked. She even checked the restaurant’s kitchen security footage to be sure. The footage showed an employee boxing a clearly uncharred pizza destined for Dana B.Masa then laid out the facts in a complaint that countered the first complaint, and the app soon reversed its automatic refund initially dispersed to the scammer. But while justice was served this time, Reynolds remains worried that the experience is only a preview of AI cons to come.

“If this is a new frontier, we’re not gonna make through to the other side if all of our time is spent [on scams],” she said.

#4508. Tesla tuner Unplugged offers to take over Cybertruck production

Unplugged Performance, the biggest name in Tesla aftermarket tuning, wants to keep the Cybertruck alive. The company publicly offered on Tuesday to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands, funded by a consortium of investors.

It comes just four days after Elon Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027, with the truck selling at roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year Tesla planned for.

UP posted the pitch on X as “an open offer to Tesla.” The company says it fully supports putting Cybercab first and would run Cybertruck production “at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus.”

In exchange, Tesla would collect a license fee plus FSD and Robotaxi network revenue on every vehicle built. UP even offered to let Cybercab get first call on battery cells. “We’ll wait our turn,” the company wrote.

UP founder Ben Schaffer made it clear that he supports Tesla’s all-in move to autonomy, but he wants to keep the Cybertruck program alive.

And it isn’t stopping at the pickup. UP says it would build the Cybertruck, a three-row “CyberSUV,” and an unmanned “CyberCargo” hauler. Two vehicles Tesla has sometimes referenced, but they were never unveiled.

The post passed 240,000 views within hours, and the replies are mostly Cybertruck owners and Tesla shareholders begging Musk to say yes. Neither Musk nor Tesla had publicly responded at the time of writing.

UP has a lot riding on this. It sells an entire Cybertruck product line, the UP Invincible lift and armor kits, and it has scored several contracts to turn Cybertrucks into police vehicles for law enforcement agencies. CEO Ben Schaffer once described the company’s purpose as doing “the things that Tesla maybe wants to do, but doesn’t have the bandwidth to do.” This is that idea taken to its extreme.

Musk framed the Cybertruck’s end as a space problem. He said Tesla needs to “make room for increased Cybercab production.”

If the Cybertruck program was successful, Tesla wouldn’t be killing it. Tesla also produces Model Ys at Giga Texas, and it is not shutting that down to make room for Cybercab.

As we reported when Tesla announced the wind-down, that explanation doesn’t hold up. Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet of floor space, the Cybertruck line runs at about a quarter of its 125,000-unit installed capacity, and Texas had only a few hundred Cybercabs registered as of late October.

The real problem is buyers. Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3, and we estimated 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks, a pace of about 30,000 trucks a year. That was a good quarter by Cybertruck standards.

Even that number flatters it. S&P Global Mobility data showed SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025, about 18% of US registrations that quarter. Tesla also tried a cheaper RWD trim, killed it, launched a $60,000 AWD version, then raised prices by $5,000 in August. None of it fixed demand.

I’ll give UP credit for this: the offer calls Musk’s bluff. If the Cybertruck is really dying because Cybercab needs the room, here’s someone volunteering to take the line off Tesla’s plate. Problem solved.

Of course, it’s more complicated than that.

There are many ways this could fail or never happen in the first place, but there’s also a slight possibility that makes this possible.

First off, the backlash is real. If you look on social media and forums, yes, most of the discussion is about how Cybertruck is a failure, and Elon is lying about why Tesla is killing it, but there’s also a serious group of people, especially Cybertruck owners, who are genuinely upset that Tesla is killing the program because they love their trucks.

Most people have never driven a Cybertruck, but the steer-by-wire makes it a very addictive vehicle to drive, and even though the price is high, the value proposition for the specs is not bad compared to the very limited options for electric pickup trucks.

In other words, I wouldn’t necessarily bet against this effort, especially if they add an SUV variant and show the program some love with some tweaks here and there.

I could see a group of wealthy Cybertruck fans pooling money under Unplugged to make this happen, but getting Tesla to agree could be hard. It’s not unheard of for an automaker to sell a vehicle program to a dealer, like the Lotus Seven and Studebaker Avanti, but it would be a first at this scale.

Who is singing up to light their cash on fire? There is just no way that would work. Unless Tesla just gave them the designs and tooling. Then they are stuck the same problem with who is their market. There are 3 ev trucks coming that are cheaper better and more practical. Likey 3 or 4 more by the end of the decade.

You could make sense of it by looking at UP to Tesla as AMG to Mercedes. It’s not too big a stretch, considering UP isn’t just your average Tesla tuner. It even worked with the automaker on its own version of the Model S Plaid.

If UP were to become for Tesla what AMG has become for Mercedes, it could make some sense for the company to run a separate vehicle program that started under Tesla, but even as I write this, I realize that there’s very little chance this will happen.

But I wish them the best of luck, and I would be happy to see the Cybertruck live on.

#4507. A Tesla Aftermarket Shop Wants to Build the Cybertruck Under License

Unplugged Performance took to Tesla boss Elon Musk’s preferred social medium of choice, X, to make the offer.

The Tesla Cybertruck, as you may well have heard by now, is on death row. How the news hits you will likely depend on what your opinions on the truck that company CEO “Technoking” Elon Musk once described as “what Bladerunner would have driven.” Those who dislike the steel-bodied machine range from pleased to gloating; fans, meanwhile, are rending garments and clutching their vowel-less vanity plates. Alas, poor Cybertruck; I knew him, Elon!

But one group of Tesla enthusiasts are aiming to take matters into their own hands. Unplugged Performance, an aftermarket shop specializing in Teslas, has taken to social media to entreat the automaker not to kill off the slab-sided pickup, but rather, to license its production out to them instead.

The company took to X—which is owned by Musk, who is also, shall we say, a vocal user—to make the offer. “An open offer to Tesla: We fully support putting Cybercab first, and we’d be glad to take the Cybertruck line off your hands. We’d fund it with a consortium of investors and run it at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus,” Unplugged Performance wrote.

That offer, unsurprisingly, evoked a reaction amongst Internet-active fans of the Cybertruck, as well as quite a few questions for specifics. To their credit, Unplugged Performance responded with a comprehensive amount of detail regarding the plan so far. “A fair question we’re hearing: can UP really run the Cybertruck vehicle line? Not alone, and not overnight,” the brand tweeted (X-ed?), before elaborating that it intends to round up investors and manufacturing partners in the months leading up to Tesla’s planned changeover of its Texas plant that will use the capacity currently occupied by the truck to build autonomous Cybercabs.

“We believe this is highly fundable because one production platform serves three markets: existing demand for the pickup, pent-up demand for a seven-seat SUV, and Robotaxi network vehicles in useful all-terrain form factors (seven-seat people movers, cargo haulers, and pickups),” Unplugged Performance continued.

“Should add,” the shop added, “the number of Tesla alumni who have reached out offering to help has been overwhelming. For anyone questioning talent or experience, we already have a strong and resourceful team, and many people who helped build these vehicles want to participate and see the platform live on.”

As of this story’s Wednesday afternoon publication, Tesla and Musk don’t appear to have offered a public response to Unplugged’s offer. That said, Musk did post on Wednesday that pickup production is being extended through summer of next year to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” And given his follow-up, who knows? Maybe he’d be open to letting someone else take over after that.

#4506. A Trip Through Toyota’s New GR Garage Experience Center

From Ivan Stewart’s Baja-winning off-road trucks to the monstrous Toyota Eagle MkIII, this collection chronicles nearly 70 years of Toyota racing history.

Toyota’s motorsports resume is a lot longer than you might expect. Long before Gazoo Racing was stamping GR badges onto Corollas, Supras, and the occasional RAV4, Toyota was racing across the Australian Outback, battling American muscle cars in IMSA, and building some of the most successful prototype racers ever to cross the finish line.

Near the Toyota Experience Center in Plano, Texas, the automaker has gathered an impressive collection of vehicles from its racing past. There’s a little bit of everything here: a 1957 Toyopet Crown that helped launch Toyota’s international racing ambitions, a legendary desert-racing pickup, a Le Mans prototype packing 1000 horsepower, and even a few cars from more recent spec series.

Here’s a look at some of the machines that helped build Toyota’s motorsports legacy at the new GR Garage Experience Center.

From the moment you walk into Toyota’s GR Experience Center, it’s obvious nearly every inch of this place has been curated to celebrate the brand’s motorsports history. Racing memorabilia, suspension components, and die-cast cars decorate the walls and many office rooms at the unassuming facility. It’s equal parts museum and shrine that honors the Japanese company’s obsession with racing.

Toyota’s international motorsports career began not with a World Rally car, but with this. In 1957, a Toyopet Crown entered the Mobilgas Round Australia Rally, an extraordinarily demanding endurance event covering thousands of miles of Australia's unforgiving landscape. The Crown finished 47th overall and third among foreign entries. They didn’t take home the trophy for first place, but surviving the 19-day endurance trial was plenty to brag about. More importantly, the experience exposed weaknesses Toyota would address in future vehicles.

Long before the Supra, there was the 2000GT. Toyota enlisted legendary American racer and car builder Carroll Shelby to develop the beautiful sports car for SCCA competition in 1968. Only three were prepared for the program, with Scooter Patrick driving the No. 33 car pictured here. The 2000GT’s 2.0-liter inline-six produced roughly 200 horsepower in racing trim, and the Shelby-prepared Toyotas proved surprisingly competitive against Porsche. Patrick finished second in the C-Production championship standings.

Don’t let the Celica badge fool you. This is about as closely related to a production Celica as a NASCAR stock car is to the sedan it resembles. Developed by Dan Gurney’s All American Racers, the IMSA GTO Celica used a tube-frame chassis, rear-wheel drive, and a heavily turbocharged inline-four engine producing as much as 600 horsepower. In 1987, Chris Cord and Toyota captured the IMSA GTO drivers’ and manufacturers’ championships. Not bad for a highly dramatized economy car.

Few vehicles are more immediately recognizable in off-road racing than Ivan “Ironman” Stewart’s red-and-white Toyota trucks. Built by Precision Preparation Inc. (PPI), these machines helped Stewart become one of the most successful drivers in desert racing history. Across his career, Stewart accumulated 84 victories and 10 championships, including 17 Baja 500 wins and three Baja 1000 victories. His nickname came from his willingness to tackle grueling desert events without a co-driver. Just imagine spending hundreds of miles bouncing around inside this thing. Sadly, most of us have only driven one of these via the Ironman “Ivan” Offroad Racing arcade game.

My absolute favorite in the room, and easily the most intimidating. Developed by Dan Gurney’s All American Racers, the Eagle MkIII competed in IMSA’s outrageously fast GTP category during the early 1990s. A turbocharged inline-four engine produced more than 800 horsepower, while its sophisticated aerodynamics generated enormous downforce. With Juan Manuel Fangio II leading the charge, the Eagle helped Toyota capture consecutive IMSA GTP manufacturers’ championships in 1992 and 1993. At one point, the Eagle won 17 consecutive races. It was so dominant that very little competition remained.

The Lexus LFA was already an engineering spectacle, thanks largely to its screaming 4.8-liter V-10. But Toyota wasn’t content to let its supercar spend its life sitting in collectors’ garages. The LFA became an important part of the early Gazoo Racing effort, participating in grueling endurance races at the Nürburgring. The program also helped Toyota develop its philosophy of using motorsports to improve road cars, with company chairman Akio Toyoda personally participating in racing and vehicle development.

Lexus decided that another 10 horses, sharper suspension, quicker shifts, and a gigantic fixed carbon-fiber wing were needed for the LFA. And they were right. The resulting Nürburgring Package was originally limited to just 50 examples. In 2011, one lapped the Nürburgring in 7:14.64, an astonishing time for a road car of its era. Just to the right of the LFA sits a Toyota Supra MkIV, the very one Toyota master driver Hiromu Naruse used to teach Akio Toyoda how to hustle a car.

Before Toyota finally conquered the 24 Hours of Le Mans, it built this legendary hybrid prototype. The TS040 combined a 3.7-liter V-8 with electric motors driving both axles, producing approximately 1000 horsepower. Rather than conventional batteries, the car used supercapacitors to store energy recovered during braking. Toyota won both the World Endurance Championship manufacturers’ and drivers’ titles in 2014, before introducing an extensively revised version of the TS040 for 2015.

The Lexus RC F GT3 seen here, yawning with its giant grille, has spent many years competing in motorsports. Its 5.4-liter V-8 engine helped Vasser Sullivan Racing become a formidable competitor in IMSA, despite facing newer, turbocharged rivals. The team captured the 2023 GTD Pro championship, with victories at Watkins Glen and Long Beach. It followed that up with a class victory at the 2024 12 Hours of Sebring. 2026 was the RC F’s final year in IMSA, and it will be replaced at the 24 Hours of Daytona in January by the GR GT3 race car.

The Supra’s return to the street also brought a new Toyota race car. Developed for customer racing in the GT4 category, the GR Supra GT4 shares its 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-six with the road-going Supra, but adds suspension, brakes, aerodynamics, and a stripped-out interior that’s only tolerable in race cars. Its initial specification produced approximately 430 horsepower, subject to racing balance-of-performance regulations. Unlike the wild prototypes elsewhere in this collection, the Supra GT4 remains closely related to something you might drive to work.

Think of the GR86 Cup Car as the affordable end of Toyota’s motorsports spectrum. Built for Toyota’s single-make GR Cup racing series, which began in 2023, the car retains the production model’s 2.4-liter flat-four engine but replaces its manual transmission with a six-speed sequential gearbox. The goal is to provide drivers with relatively accessible, closely matched machinery that emphasizes driving talent instead of checkbook size. Plus, it’s one of the few cars in the museum that you can also drive in iRacing.

Developed for SRO’s TC America touring-car championship, the GR Corolla TC starts with Toyota’s 300-hp, turbocharged 1.6-liter three-cylinder engine and retains the GR-Four all-wheel-drive system. Interestingly, it also uses the production car’s eight-speed automatic transmission. The transformation includes upgraded suspension, Alcon brakes, a roll cage, and aggressive aerodynamic bodywork.

#4505. It’s that time again – Honda needs to roll out an electric Super Cub

Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.

I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub. Not another futuristic concept with swoopy bodywork and a name that looks like a Wi-Fi password. I mean an actual honest-to-goodness Honda Super Cub, except electric.

The formula is already sitting right there.

The Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958. It’s still in continuous production today.

And a huge part of that success comes down to how approachable the thing is. It isn’t supposed to be intimidating, excessively powerful, or particularly complicated. It’s simple, practical transportation wrapped in one of the most recognizable two-wheeler designs ever created.

In other words, it’s practically begging to become electric.

The beauty of the bike is how simple and timeless it is, with the appearance barely changing in nearly 7 decades. And with the design freedom that electric drivetrains provide, upgrading the cute little bike to an electric future would be a walk in the park for Honda’s engineers.

An in-wheel motor would be a simple, cheap solution that frees up even more space in the body for batteries.

And Honda wouldn’t need some enormous battery capable of highway touring. Give an electric Super Cub enough battery for perhaps 50-60 miles (80-95 km) of real-world urban riding, a motor capable of roughly 50-60 mph (80-95 km/h), and simple Level 1 charging from a normal wall outlet. As a city runabout or a beachside cruiser, those middle-of-the-road specs would be perfect.

Even better, make the battery removable. Honda already has its Mobile Power Pack e: swappable battery system used in various electric two-wheelers, and an electric Super Cub would be an incredible platform to expand it.

The resulting bike could hit an unusually sweet spot.

There are millions of people riding electric bicycles today who will eventually want something faster, but don’t necessarily want a 500-pound (220 kg) electric motorcycle capable of hitting 120 mph (200 km/h). An electric Super Cub would be a natural next step: light, unintimidating, easy to ride, cheap to operate, and fast enough to actually function as a real urban vehicle.

It would also be one of the rare electric motorcycles that could appeal to people who aren’t necessarily looking for an “electric motorcycle.” An electric version is in such high demand that companies specialize in retrofit kits to convert classic Cubs into EVs.

The Super Cub already has decades of cultural cachet. It’s cute. It’s useful. It’s nostalgic without feeling ancient. It’s the kind of motorcycle that can appeal equally to a lifelong rider and someone who has never considered owning a motorcycle before.

And perhaps most importantly, Honda could actually sell the thing globally. The same basic electric Super Cub could work in dense European cities, throughout Asia, and in American cities and suburbs. It doesn’t need to win spec-sheet battles. It just needs to be affordable, reliable, and unmistakably a Super Cub.

As soon as Honda makes an electric scooter or motorcycle that could come close to replacing my Honda Silverwing, I am buying it. I need at least 80 miles of range at 50-55 mph. If it had a swappable battery I could carry with me, I'd be in Heaven. I think they have something like this in Asia, but not North America. Please.

Honda has already shown that it understands the importance of electrifying small two-wheelers. It’s even made a token gesture with a Cub-like e-scooter in China. But there’s a difference between making another electric scooter and electrifying perhaps the most famous small motorcycle ever made.

You’ve got the name. You’ve got the design. You’ve got the batteries. You’ve got the manufacturing scale.

Just put all the pieces together and give us the electric Super Cub already. The world is waiting, and will thank you.

#4504. Endangered, colorful garter snakes released into the wild for the first time

Published Nov 12, 2026 4:08 PM EST

Most people have never seen a San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia). Native only to California’s San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties, the brilliantly colored reptile was one of the initial entries in the United States Fish and Wildlife Service’s first endangered species list in 1967. After nearly 60 more years of droughts, invasive species, disease, low genetic diversity, and poaching, researchers estimate only a few thousand San Francisco garter snakes still exist in the wild.

However, conservationists recently scored a major win for the snakes. For the first time, 62 of young serpents born at the San Francisco Zoo were released at specific sites across San Mateo County earlier this fall. The successful rewilding of dozens of the endangered snakes marks a huge moment for population rehabilitation efforts, and hopefully clears the way for similar releases in the future.

“Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen) biologist Karine Tokatlian said in a statement. “This first release is an important step toward building healthy, resilient populations that can sustain themselves over the long term.”

Although slender, the brightly colored San Francisco garter snake can grow anywhere from 18 to 55 inches long. Its eyes are larger than most of its fellow garter snakes, allowing it to keep active during daylight hours. With no fangs and only mildly toxic saliva, the snake is essentially harmless to humans, although its bites are fatal for prey like smaller reptiles and rodents.

The process of releasing young animals like these snakes that were reared in captivity is known as head-starting. It is an effective way to protect creatures during the most vulnerable stage of their lives. Head-starting the first batch of San Francisco garter snakes began in 2025, when conservationists collected multiple pregnant females from a healthy preserve in California’s Midpeninsula. Researchers later released the adult snakes back into their habitats after they gave birth, but kept the infants at the San Francisco Zoo. While there, zoologists conducted genetic testing on each snake to select the best possible locations for their eventual release. Conservationists deposited about one-third of them in the same area as their mothers, then placed the other two-thirds at locations particularly in need of greater genetic diversity pools for breeding.

As biologists continue to monitor the first generation of head-started snakes, another generation is already waiting for its time to shine. More than 130 garter snakes have been born at the San Francisco Zoo this year alone, with an eye to release them sometime in 2027.

“This species is special in many ways, but unfortunately its critical status is not unique,” added Midpen wildlife ecologist Ariel Starr. “The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species.”

#4503. 2028 Honda CR-V Will Go Hybrid-Only, Debut a New Platform

The new “Honda Hybrid” system is more efficient, increases power, and comes paired with an electric AWD setup.

We’re not done with 2026 quite yet, but the 2028 Honda CR-V is already coming in hot. On Thursday, the brand offered up its first official details about the next-gen version of the company’s highly important crossover—and big changes are in stow

First off, the 2028 model will be a complete redesign: underpinned by a new platform, boasting a fresh design inside and out, and powered by a new “Honda Hybrid” system. Not only is the hybrid new, but it will be the only powertrain choice available for the seventh-gen CR-V. This hybrid-only approach follows in the successful footsteps of the current Toyota RAV4, Honda’s biggest rival in the compact SUV segment.

When it comes to details, Honda is being purposely vague, but still giving us a few items to chew on. The new platform this CR-V will ride on increases body rigidity and reduces weight compared to the current car. It also has greater modularity built in, which Honda says will allow for greater parts commonality between models.

The Honda Hybrid powertrain itself will build on the two-motor hybrid system we’ve seen for years. Honda says it’s aiming for a 10-percent improvement to fuel efficiency gained by expanding the range where the engine operates most efficiently and an increase in the efficiency of the hybrid unit. More power is promised from the four-cylinder Atkinson cycle engine, and we’ll also see a new electric AWD system make its debut on this CR-V. Per usual, Honda is also claiming the CR-V will bring further enhancements to the “joy of driving,” which is always heartening to hear.

A single image of the new CR-V logo on a dark metallic blue paint was provided as a teaser. It’s rather edgy in appearance, far more so than the current logo’s font. We suspect this new sharper logo design will translate into the rest of the car, but Honda is holding back from showing us the SUV’s design for now.

This next-gen CR-V will continue to be built in North America with production spread out across three plants, two in the U.S. and one in Canada.

#4502. Tested: 2027 Mercedes-Benz CLA350 EV Aims High and Nearly Hits the Mark

Mercedes brings some luxury elements to a lower price point, but not always the right ones.

The glamour of a Mercedes, the ease and efficiency of an electric drivetrain, and an affordable price tag: That’s the premise of Mercedes-Benz’s entry-level CLA-class, which offers some of the same high-end features found on Mercedes’s big nameplates in a smaller, more cost-effective package. It’s an ambitious goal, and the electric 2027 CLA350 hits some of its selling points better than others, but it doesn’t cross everything off the list.

The CLA’s exterior styling would be most politely described as “ovoid elegance.” Think Fabergé on wheels, with intricately detailed LED headlights and a plethora of three-pointed stars, including a massive, illuminated badge in the center of the grille. If you’re paying to make sure people know it’s a Mercedes, you’re getting your money’s worth; not only is the center badge surrounded by 142 twinkly little light-up stars, but the 18- and 19-inch wheel options, the taillights, and the decklid all don Mercedes’s cosmic callouts too.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94109

Like a Fabergé, the CLA350 hopes to dazzle with interior details as well, so the cabin features illuminated climate control vents, door panels, and a center console with floating architectural details. Reflecting it all on our tester is a dash-wide Superscreen display, part of the top-range $5850 Pinnacle Line trim package. On cars without the optional passenger screen, there’s a polished star-studded panel on the right side to make sure there’s no corner of the CLA that isn’t glossy and glassy.

The downside of all this sculptural interior design is a loss of cabin space. The door panels and seat controls protrude inward, and the console sits high in the center, its harder plastic points exerting a gravitational pull to elbows and knees. The seats are comfortable and adjustable, but there are so many less forgiving surfaces surrounding the seating areas that the cabin can feel claustrophobic, like trying to sit on the couch in an overly decorated house. There’s a real fear of knocking over a vase. Things don’t improve in the rear seat, which we also found cramped. It’ll do in a pinch, but it is a pinch, especially for tall passengers or bulky child safety seats. Too bad folks can’t ride in the cargo area, which offers a deep-set 10 cubic feet in the rear and a single snack-sized cube in the frunk.

Despite the danger to funny bones, the CLA is an enjoyable driving experience. The 350 is a more powerful version of the 268-hp CLA250+ model, combining a 107-hp front motor and a 242-hp rear unit for all-wheel drive, 349 horsepower, and 380 pound-feet of torque. A two-speed transmission on the rear axle helps make power delivery more efficient, especially during highway drives. At the test track, the dual-motor 350 outran the 250+ with a quarter-mile time of 12.9 seconds compared to the single-motor’s 14.5-second run. It’s quicker from the get-go, taking only 4.3 seconds to hit 60 mph, as opposed to the CLA250+’s 5.8 seconds. Neither CLA is headed for racetrack domination, but the CLA350 makes short work of freeway merges.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94109

Ride quality isn’t as plush as it is in higher-priced Mercedes offerings, but we found the CLA quiet and comfortable with responsive steering, an easy way to commute. Adjustable brake regeneration settings allow for all manner of operation, from fully fledged one-pedal driving to a barely-there glide. We liked that last choice the best, as it offered a nice mix of brake assist while allowing enough creep to move through stop-and-go traffic naturally. In terms of grip, the CLA came to a halt from 70 mph in 161 feet, and it exhibited some moderate understeer around the skidpad, where it pulled 0.85 g of stick.

Rather than all-out performance, Mercedes’s main focus with the CLA is tech and software. It’s a screen-based cabin, with data spread across a 10.3-inch gauge cluster, a 14.0-inch touchscreen, and (if so optioned) in a head-up display and a second 14.0-inch screen in front of the passenger. We’ve yet to run into a passenger who wants to poke at their unflattering reflection in any of these new passenger-side screens, but if your guests would rather watch Disney+ than converse, that’s now a possibility.

Another trend that’s found its way down the price range is adjustable cabin mood lighting. In the CLA, a pastel glow runs in strips along the dash and doors and circles the air vents in customizable colors. Actual sunlight, if you’re so inclined, can be softly filtered through the panoramic glass roof with the optional $1050 Sky Control electrochromic transparency feature, which adjusts opacity for the whole roof or in stylish striped segments. Other fancy-feeling features include an automatic trunk close (part of the Pinnacle trim), a center airbag, and the option for a 16-speaker Burmester 3D surround-sound stereo.

Many of these high-end additions are welcome, but Mercedes also made some strange decisions here. We would have happily sacrificed the mood lighting in exchange for massaging seats, a standard heated steering wheel, or—perhaps most of all—four window switches, rather than two switches and a toggle to control the rear doors. On the same theme of “just give us a button,” controls for lumbar support and climate settings are buried in the center screen, making adjustments finicky once you’ve embarked.

It’s not that these controls aren’t usable, but using them inspires a slight resentment toward the designer every time. The most egregious of these in-screen interfaces is the lack of a “skip track” option on the steering wheel. Instead of subtly passing over Cardi B’s WAP while ferrying your mother to her chiropractor, you’ve now got to scramble into the settings, or even worse, shout at the voice control to fast forward before Mom asks what WAP stands for. That is not a luxury experience.

If the CLA falls short on the infotainment user experience, it makes up ground when it comes to charging and range. Both CLA variants use an 800-volt architecture with an 85-kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) battery and a 320-kW DC fast-charge peak rate. We haven’t had a chance to do our real-world range test on the 350 yet, but it’s EPA-rated at 312 miles of range, and Mercedes says it should recharge from 10 to 80 percent in about 22 minutes. The 250+ model beat its official range estimate in our testing, so we wouldn’t be surprised if the 350 impresses as well.

The CLA delivers handily on the promise of electric performance and efficiency. Glamour is more subjective, but the CLA offers numerous options for interior materials and additional cosmetic packages to set it apart from the average transportation pod. At its starting point, it’s even affordable, but our test car’s reasonable $51,950 base price shot up fast with add-on features. It’s a rough world when $67,980 (as-tested) is an entry-level price and doesn’t even get you leather upholstery. It’s no S-class, but what do you expect from the opposite side of the alphabet?

Like many girls, she planned to be a vet-astronaut-artist, and came closest to that last one by attending UCLA art school. She painted images of cars, but did not own one. Elana reluctantly got a driver’s license at age 21 and discovered that she not only loved cars and wanted to drive them, but that other people loved cars and wanted to read about them, which meant somebody had to write about them. Since receiving activation codes, Elana has written for numerous car magazines and websites, covering classics, car culture, technology, motorsports, and new-car reviews. #4501. Apple HomeView smart home hub review: Siri gets a swanky new house

Published Nov 12, 2026 6:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

Apple’s $299 smart display has been sitting on my kitchen counter for about a week. It looks like a hybrid between an old-school iMac and a giant Apple Watch, but it’s a dedicated home for the recently revamped Siri. It’s an easy addition for anyone already committed to Apple gear. If your smart home runs on cameras, locks, or sensors that don’t work with Apple Home, though, you’ll want an upgrade plan before you buy one.

The HomeView comes in two versions, and both cost $299 in the US. I tested the tabletop model, which mounts a 7-inch square touchscreen on a domed aluminum speaker base and includes a 30W power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. You can have it in any color you want, as long as it’s silver, starlight, rose pink, or space gray. The Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) drops the base and its extra speaker hardware, as well as the starlight/rose pink color options, and the panel costs more to put on a wall than its sticker price suggests. It requires a Schneider Home mount sold separately, and those start at $59.95. The cheapest USB-C mount also needs a power adapter of at least 20W, which you’ll have to supply yourself.

The HomeView looks the way you’d expect an Apple product to look. Once you take off the protective coverings, the 2.1-pound, 6.82-inch tall device is pretty right out of the box. And it looks great between a breadbox and a butcher’s block, especially compared to an older smart screen that I’ve had there for years, which looks ancient next to it. A stainless steel hinge connects the screen to the base, so you can tilt the display toward wherever you’re standing. The screen stays firmly in place after you position it, even if you tap aggressively like I tend to. It doesn’t wobble or shake as you navigate on-screen menus.

Setting up the HomeView feels like setting up an iPhone or any other recent Apple device. It requires an iPhone running iOS 27.2 or later (or an iPad on iPadOS 27.2), so if your phone isn’t there yet, like mine wasn’t, you’ve got to stop and run the update first. The HomeView played a soft, heavenly drone the whole time it waited, which is a much nicer way to sit through a software update than staring at a progress bar. Also, when you first boot things up, you might think you can immediately start asking for the kind of stuff you ask Siri on your iPhone, but you may have to go through a round or two of launching apps on the HomeView to give them permission to access your account even if your iPhone is with you.

The HomeView’s Liquid Retina LED backlit screen has looked great in every lighting condition I’ve put it in. Apple rates the 1088-by-1088-pixel (220 ppi) display’s brightness between 0.3 and 500 nits, and that bottom end is what makes it work on a nightstand. In a dark kitchen, it reads as a soft glow instead of a floodlight.

The multitouch True Tone touchscreen responds quickly, and it kept registering taps even when my fingers were slightly wet (even though the device doesn’t have a specific water-resistance rating). That’s a real advantage for a screen that spends its life in a kitchen.

The new, more conversational Siri AI on the HomeView is a big jump from the old Siri. The HomeView’s four-mic design ensures Siri can hear you from throughout the room and, when a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone is nearby, it can pull from personal data. If you ask about an upcoming concert, it can also check the calendar on your Apple account and tell whether you’re actually free to go.

That personal access runs through the HomeView’s 12MP Center Stage camera. It can recognize up to six Home app-registered household members by face, and it only shows someone’s personal information when it recognizes that person and their paired iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network—with support for Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO—and was recently unlocked. The HomeView’s A18 chip uses what Apple calls Secure Exclaves to process the camera and microphone feeds in a separate compartment, and Apple says neither the operating system nor Apple itself can access it. Those safeguards are reassuring on paper, though they aren’t something I could independently verify while testing a smart display in my kitchen.

That reliance on a nearby iPhone or iPad is also the source of the HomeView’s most frustrating quirk. With my phone on me, Siri sometimes can’t decide which device should answer. The first few times I tried to set a simple timer, it turned into a dance between the HomeView and my phone before one of them finally took the request. It takes a little getting used to.

Your iPhone also supplies a big share of the HomeView’s apps. There’s no App Store on the device. It ships with 15 built-in apps, including Safari, FaceTime, Music, and Home, and it pulls a handful of other Apple apps, like TV and News, from your phone. So, if you don’t mind some severe letterboxing, you can watch TV and movies on there. Supported third-party audio and video apps show up from a paired iPhone, too, through a system that works a lot like CarPlay. If a service you rely on doesn’t support it, there’s no way to install it on the HomeView directly.

The HomeView’s main job is running your smart home, and that’s where my experience was most mixed. It controls accessories you’ve added to Apple Home, which includes supported HomeKit and Matter devices. My Ring cameras don’t integrate with Apple Home natively, so they never appeared in the HomeView’s Home Camera face, which can otherwise show up to nine live feeds at once. It worked easily with my smart lighting and other natively compatible devices.

Check whether your current cameras, locks, sensors, and thermostat show up in Apple Home before you plan to run the whole house from this screen. If they don’t, budget for HomeKit or Matter replacements that do (and Apple has a whole suite of new options developed alongside LG and Schneider Electric).

The actual smart hub interface that displays on screen is handy for keeping tabs on what’s going on in your home. It’s important to note that this thing looks like a thermostat when it’s on the wall, but it isn’t one. Maybe a future model with a built-in thermostat could free up some wall space.

The HomeView turned out to be a great cooking assistant. Once you open a recipe page on the web, either on your iPhone or in Safari on the HomeView, a Start Cooking button reformats it so you can follow the steps in real time while you work. Recipe pages vary wildly in how they’re formatted and coded, and I expected that mess to trip it up. It has worked without a problem every time I’ve used it so far.

I made a fairly simple recipe for peanut butter noodles, and the instructions and timers were helpful and easy to use. More complicated recipes are more of a challenge, especially since you can’t really perform more than one step at a time, so don’t expect it to turn you into Gordon Ramsay overnight.

As for the audio, the tabletop HomeView sounds full for its size. Its base holds a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators, almost like a subwoofer in miniature (but without the extension), and the display adds two custom full-range down-firing drivers of its own. I’d been using an older Google smart display before this, and the jump in sound quality is obvious.

In separate tests, PopSci editor Tony Ware spent a couple of nights with his own HomeView and some of his favorite songs and came away with positive impressions. Compared to a HomePod mini, the beat hits more convincingly. While there’s not much room for excursion in the base, output manages to be surprisingly potent without sacrificing clarity. It won’t beat some recent whole-home audio-focused connected speakers (or Apple’s own full-sized 2nd-gen. HomePod, for that matter), but it’s plenty room-filling for such a compact, multipurpose enclosure. Whether you’re chopping carrots or choppin’ it up with friends, the HomeView is more than enough speaker for a smaller space.

What was more impressive was the airy, open presence of Dolby Atmos tracks from Apple Music, given the use of reflections and computational audio rather than an actual array of directional drivers. With accelerometers and Apple silicon adjusting the acoustic system’s EQ and output based on the screen’s tilt, the result is more incisive than immersive … how it will always be when you can’t surround yourself with speakers. Still, it projects clearly without sounding overly bright or edgy, which is good for podcasts to playlists.

There are occasional kinks, however. If you’re into spatial audio, the best way to ensure you’re getting the correct version of a track is to ask the HomeView to pull Apple Music directly from the cloud; sometimes the Dolby Atmos badge won’t pop up when you send a track from your phone over AirPlay, so you can’t be certain it’s not just stereo. Alternatively, you can hand off whatever is playing on your phone by bringing it close enough to the HomeView to get an AirDrop ripple animation and the album art to show up. Also, you might find yourself instinctively running your finger along the edge of the display looking for volume buttons, but there are no physical controls, which isn’t surprising from an aesthetic standpoint but still feels like a shortcoming.

The Apple HomeView makes the most sense on a nightstand, on the wall next to your thermostat, or in the kitchen. Its Photos face turns it into a digital picture frame, which keeps it from looking like a giant Apple Watch stuck to your wall or sitting on your table (though the clock faces are cute and colorful).

If your home already runs on an iPhone and Apple Home accessories, HomeView slots right in and puts it all on one screen you’ll actually want to look at. If you’ve built your smart home around gear that doesn’t work with Apple Home, however, plan to replace it before you make the jump.

#4500. QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

QuantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state. Its new Osprey platform swaps the liquid in its cathode for a sulfide solid electrolyte, and the company says the cells have hit 1,000 full cycles to 80% capacity at just one atmosphere of pressure.

That’s a big deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial. Their cells typically need heavy clamping to work. But the white paper behind the announcement shows these are small, early lab cells, and some headline numbers come with important conditions.

Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.

The new white paper describes the QSE platform, including the QSE-5 cell it’s shipping as samples from its Eagle Line pilot production in San Jose, as a ceramic separator paired with “a relatively conventional high-nickel NMC cathode and a liquid catholyte.”

The solid part is the separator. It sits between the cathode and a lithium-metal anode that QuantumScape doesn’t manufacture at all. The cell is built “anode-free,” and lithium plates against the separator during the first charge.

Osprey keeps that separator and anode-free design and swaps the liquid in the cathode for a solid sulfide electrolyte. That makes the whole cell solid.

The interesting part is that QuantumScape hasn’t changed its mind on sulfides. It has spent years arguing that sulfide electrolytes can’t work as separators, and the white paper doubles down, calling their problems “fundamental properties” of the material rather than engineering challenges.

The company lists four issues: sulfides react with lithium metal, they need high pressure to keep contact with the electrodes, they struggle at room temperature and below, and they can’t handle fast charging with a lithium-metal anode before dendrites form.

The pressure point is the one automakers care about most. QuantumScape illustrates it this way: 20 atm on a single 10 x 24.2 cm cell works out to roughly 5,000 kg of force, about three mid-size cars. Holding that across a pack takes thick steel end plates and tie rods, which add weight, volume, and cost.

And 20 atm is on the generous side. Many sulfide cells in labs run at 30 to 100+ atm (3 to 12 MPa), and some even higher. China’s FAW reported large-format sulfide cells cycling at 5 MPa, or about 50 atm, in September, which was billed as a low-pressure achievement.

So QS’s pitch is simple: keep the sulfide in the cathode, where it’s good at moving lithium ions, and let the QS ceramic separator handle the lithium metal.

QuantumScape published four main data sets:

This is the strongest result. A 2-layer cell with a 50 x 65 mm cathode, the same area as QSE-5, ran 1,000 cycles to about 80% capacity. The test used full 1C charge and 1C discharge, 0 to 100% state of charge, 30°C, and 1 atm. The cathode loading was 5.5 mAh/cm², which is in line with commercial EV cells.

QuantumScape says no other sulfide-based cell has shown this, and Electrek couldn’t find published data that contradicts it. Academic groups have shown sulfide cells running with little or no external pressure, but not for 1,000 full cycles with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode.

But this is a small cell. By our math, two layers at that size come out to roughly 0.3 to 0.4 Ah, compared to about 5 Ah for a QSE-5.

The press release says “five-minute fast charging from 10% to 80%.” The white paper shows that was achieved at 10C, in a 2-layer cell, at 80°C (176°F). The chart itself is captioned “High temperature enables 5 min fast charge.”

Batteries charge much faster when hot, and EVs do precondition packs before fast charging. Still, 80°C is well above what EV packs are usually preconditioned to before a fast charge. QS didn’t publish a room-temperature fast-charge result.

“Operational down to -20°C” came from a single-layer cell with a 21 x 21 mm cathode, discharged slowly at C/3. It kept 68% of its room-temperature capacity at -20°C (about 52% of its energy) and 85% at 0°C.

That’s a real result for a sulfide system, which have historically needed heat. But it’s a tiny cell at a gentle rate.

The “up to ~1,100 Wh/L” figure is a projection. QS says high-loading cathodes (10 mAh/cm², about double today’s EV cells) are possible with sulfide catholytes. The test backing that up used an 11 mm coin-size cell at 3 atm, not 1 atm, and ran for 100 cycles.

For reference, QSE-5 is rated at 844 Wh/L and 301 Wh/kg.

QuantumScape is pitching Osprey as an “open platform.” Customers can use QS’s own sulfide cathode, made with a proprietary dry process, or bring their own. QS says it has already tested Osprey with solid cathodes developed by its automotive customers.

In other words, after years of being the sulfide skeptic, QuantumScape now wants to sell its separator and anode-free design to the companies that have spent billions developing sulfide cathodes.

That fits the licensing model it already uses with Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Honda. QS reported $9.8 million in customer billings in Q3 and announced a 100 MWh production line targeting start of production in 2028 for QSE-5.

There’s no timeline for Osprey. The white paper says the process has been demonstrated “at laboratory scale,” that higher-throughput processes are “in the development stage,” and that “significant work remains in process engineering.” Automakers also want larger prismatic cells than QSE-5, which means more layers and more area per layer.

Everyone else is on the clock. Samsung SDI is targeting mass production of sulfide all-solid-state cells in its Ulsan plant in the second half of 2027. BYD plans small-batch sulfide solid-state production in 2027, with mass production toward the end of the decade. Toyota is aiming for 2027 to 2028, after slipping from 2020, 2023, and 2026. Factorial’s sulfide Solstice platform is targeting up to 450 Wh/kg.

CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, said in June that true mass-market solid-state is still “years away,” around 2030.

None of those companies has published 1,000-cycle data at 1 atm with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode. That’s QuantumScape’s opening shot.

This is the most interesting thing QuantumScape has published in a while. The numbers are good, but the strategy shift probably stands out most.

The cycle-life result is legit. A 2-layer cell with commercial-area electrodes and realistic loading doing 1,000 full 1C cycles at 1 atm and 30°C is the kind of data the industry hasn’t shown. And QS published the test conditions, which is more than many of its competitors do.

Key thing to remember is that this is a lab test cell. There's a long road ahead to mass manufacturing.

Also, when it hopefully hits the market it will be an incremental improvement, not a quantum leap. Current cells are already in the market doing things like 5 minute charging.

But you can argue the press release oversells what’s in the white paper. A 5-minute charge at 80°C isn’t the same thing as a 5-minute charge, and the release should have said so. The energy density is projected, the cold-weather result is from a cell the size of a postage stamp, and 80% after 1,000 cycles is well below the 95% after 1,000 cycles PowerCo confirmed in QSE’s early cells back in 2024. Different chemistry, different stage, but something worth keeping in mind.

So QuantumScape is essentially admitting the liquid catholyte in QSE isn’t the end game, and that the industry’s massive sulfide investment is something to plug into rather than fight. If your separator is the one part everyone else can’t make work, selling it to them is smart.

The question is time. QS is still scaling QSE-5, with a 100 MWh line not due until 2028. Osprey is a lab process. Will anyone in the sulfide camp license it before their own 2027 to 2030 production plans lock in? At this point, it sounds like this is QS’ bet right now.

#4499. Driven: Porsche 911 Challenge Is a More Accessible Race Car

Many track cars are intimidating, to say the least. Not Porsche’s latest.

Next year will mark the 40th running of the Porsche Mobil 1 Supercup, the one-make race series so ubiquitous you hardly need either Porsche or 911 qualifiers for somebody to know what you mean by “Cup car.” Like other sports cars with long histories, the further you go back in time, the more similar the racing 911 is to the roadgoing version. Likewise, the further forward you move, the more they diverge.

Early 964 Cup cars are, like Ferrari’s 355 Challenge, road legal with normal VIN codes. They were stripped, caged versions of standard Carreras. I’m leaving out a lot of hardworking engineers’ tweaks here, but the point is that there was a time that driving a Cup car felt mostly like a normal car with more noise, fewer comforts, and better safety equipment. The 1999 996-generation Cup still used a coded key and had a normal clutch and an H-pattern 6-speed—it was just a very sticky GT3. But the 997 generation of 2005 was the fork in the road, introducing a sequential gearbox. The 2013 991-gen brought in a motorsport engine-management system and electronics. And the 992 generation that races today nominally resembles a 911 but operates nothing like one and requires a team to run it.

I tried the 992 Cup Car. It is incredibly intimidating. I do not have what it takes to be successful in a car like that, and I would not want to have to round up a posse to go for a drive, even if the performance is staggering. Instead what I really want, as do many other amateur and wannabe racers, is a race car that closely resembles their road car. Hence the popularity of the GT3 RS. If the car never leaves the track property, why get a GT3 RS when you could get an Oreca LMP for $100k less? Because it’s not really about being street legal; it’s about being approachable and turnkey.

The car for regular weekend warriors used to be the GT4/RS Clubsport, but sadly, the 718-generation Cayman is now dead and buried. Earlier this year, rumors swirled that Porsche was prepping a 911 GT4 to take the Cayman’s place, and the story ran alongside photos of a racy-looking camouflaged 992 GT3. It turns out that Porsche is going GT4 racing with the 911, but that will be a modified Cup car, not the one from those pictures. Instead, the images were of the car you see here, the new 911 Challenge. Essentially, it’s the old GT3 Cup car concept for today’s country-club weekend warriors: an upfitted, stripped, and caged GT3 road car.

A roll cage can only make a car so approachable, but once I’d stopped and crawled into the comfy seat, things got familiar quickly, as I was looking at the complete 992-generation dashboard, gauge cluster, and center console. The steering wheel is straight out of the GT3 RS (though without an airbag installed). After strapping in with the multipoint harnesses,I pressed the original start button on the left, and the 4.0-liter flat-six fired just like a standard GT3. The Challenge retains the factory heating and ventilation; the road car’s touchscreen display is gone, replaced by a blank panel with emergency cutoff and fire switches.

Mechanically, it’s barely changed from the GT3. The engine makes six more horsepower, now 508 hp total, thanks to a race-specific exhaust setup. But it still uses the standard, seven-speed PDK dual-clutch transmission, so you can just put it in drive if you prefer, or shift using the paddles.

My drive in the Challenge was brief. Just four laps around the 2.5-mile Circuit Ricardo Tormo, following on from my four-car Manthey test. For context, with factory race driver Timo Bernhard driving this circuit, the Challenge almost perfectly splits the range: 4.6 seconds per lap slower than a Cup, and 5.2 seconds quicker than a GT3 Weissach. Notably, it’s also 1.6 seconds quicker per lap than the GT3 RS Manthey. Where it gets interesting is in the details.

A GT3 RS Manthey is on road-legal tires but with enormous downforce. The Challenge is on slicks but with the same aero package as a standard GT3.

So if you’re willing to throw away street legality, for $275,000 (less than the cost of many standard GT3s) you can go far quicker on a track than you could with the fastest road-legal 911 you can buy, the Manthey GT3 RS, which would knock on the door of half a million dollars.

Everything about the Challenge is easy. As long as you’re reasonably comfortable on a slick tire, the rest of the car comes directly to you. The Challenge is far more reliant on mechanical grip than downforce, so you can start learning the car by going much quicker through hairpins than you ever have before, rather than having to learn it by going full send over a blind crest in sixth gear, with potentially scary consequences.

Likewise, because there isn’t 2200 pounds of downforce, the Challenge isn’t sprung too stiffly, so you don’t take abuse on bumpy curbing. The knobs for traction control and PTV work essentially the same as the GT3 RS, just with new programming specific to the Challenge.

I’m not going to pretend, in five laps, to have a thorough understanding of the dynamics of the 911 Challenge, or to say that I took it to its limit. I had just enough time to get comfortable, which is more than I can say about other race cars.

What I did have was an incredible time on the track. The Challenge is the kind of car that inspired me to want to push it harder, but the “race car” bits of it disappeared into the background, so I could focus on things happening outside rather than things inside. It was instantly comfortable and familiar, and a place I could spend all day. Three-hour double stint in an enduro? That would be no problem. Also, possible thanks to the 29-gallon fuel cell.

There will be a one-make series for the 911 Challenge, and initially Porsche wants to sell them to folks who intend to enter, but that’s not really the point—this is the 911 race car that most 911 owners actually want. It is a fun, flexible, approachable, and fizzy experience that elevates what they already love about the 911 and can race if they want to, but that won’t require a whole team if they just want to rip off a few laps after work. And for less money than the road car, not more.

It’s the race car for people who want their race car to feel like a 911, not like a corporation.
