The Bronco Raptor takes the already highly capable Bronco platform and cranks up the intensity across the board: the twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 is good for 418 ponies, the beefed-up suspension features Fox adaptive dampers and a slightly wider track, and it rolls on standard 37-inch BFGoodrich K02 all-terrain tires. If that sounds like the ideal recipe for blasting through the desert, performing low-level aerial maneuvers, and breaking trails, well, that’s the point.

But arguably the most impressive thing about the Bronco Raptor is how well it settles down in less demanding situations—like your drive home from the off-road park. There’s room for five, it comes equipped with contemporary technology and infotainment, and it looks the business whether you’re in the urban jungle or the real one.

Expert Tip: The Bronco Raptor packs a lot of physical and visual punch, but at a cost. Savvy shoppers can build an impressively capable off-road beast on the bones of the base Bronco for thousands less by picking the right options.

The 2027 Bronco Raptor is largely unchanged; minor standard updates include ambient footwell lighting and a 5G modem.

Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.

Ford didn't put a V-8 in the Bronco Raptor, but it did manage to coax 418 horsepower from the twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 under the hood. The engine pairs exclusively with a 10-speed automatic transmission and an advanced four-wheel-drive system that works in concert with selectable drive modes named with the clever acronym "G.O.A.T." (Goes Over Any Type of Terrain).

The Bronco Raptor has a beefier suspension setup than the standard SUV, with a wider track, Fox adaptive dampers from the F-150 Raptor, and standard 37-inch BFGoodrich K02 all-terrain tires—all of which endow it with better high-speed stability for fast desert running, high-jumping sand dunes, and powering through rough off-road trails.

During our test drive, we were impressed with the Bronco Raptor's off-road prowess, both when bounding over bumpy terrain at speed and while crawling through rocky passes with the low-range gearing engaged.

In Comparison: While the Bronco Raptor’s twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 doesn't have the same shove as the F-150 Raptor's boosted 3.5-liter, it has enough punch to get the Bronco Raptor to 60 mph in 5.6 seconds. The F-150 Raptor hits the mark in 5.2 seconds.

In Comparison: The last Jeep Wrangler 392 we tested left the Bronco Raptor in the dust, hitting 60 mph in 4.0 seconds.

In Comparison: The Raptor can tow more than the regular Bronco—which has a maximum tow rating of 3500 pounds—but it’s still no match for Jeep’s and Toyota’s 4x4s. A V-8 Wrangler can tug a 5,000-pound trailer behind its bumper, while the 4Runner is good for 6000 pounds.

The Ford Bronco Raptor earns EPA ratings of 15 mpg city, 16 mpg highway, and 15 mpg combined. On our 75-mph highway fuel-economy route, the Bronco Raptor surprised us by returning 17 mpg—one mpg more than expected. For more information about the Bronco Raptor's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

In Comparison: Compared to the 470-hp 6.4-liter V-8 Jeep Wrangler 392, the Bronco Raptor has a marginal two-mpg advantage in city driving; both are EPA-rated for 16-mpg highway.

First Row: The extra-capable Raptor shares its purposeful interior design and its dimensions with the regular Bronco and comes standard with rubberized flooring, marine-grade vinyl upholstery, and a set of overhead auxiliary toggle switches. Those who want a more luxurious cabin can opt for leather-trimmed seats.

Second Row: The Bronco Raptor is a four-door-only proposition, and the second row offers more leg-, shoulder, and hip room than the two-door versions. Two adults will be perfectly happy sitting in the back of the Bronco Raptor, but even with the additional space, three would be a squeeze.

Cargo Capacity: The cargo hold is pretty sizable, with a claimed volume of 38.3 cubic feet behind the second row. It can fit all the SUV’s removable doors behind the back seats, but we recommend using the available protective bags to keep them safe, and they consume every inch of the cargo area when doing so.

The Bronco Raptor has a 12.0-inch vertically oriented touchscreen, running Ford's latest Sync 4 software. The infotainment system supports wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto functions, too. A one-time purchase activates seven years of unlimited Wi-Fi hotspot service, connected navigation, audio and video streaming, Alexa voice assistant, and other entertainment options. There's a rack built into the top of its dashboard for mounting smartphones and GoPros, which can be plugged into nearby 12-volt outlets; there’s also a 120-volt household outlet.

The Bronco Raptor comes standard with lots of driver-assistance technology, from blind-spot monitoring to lane-keeping assist to adaptive cruise control.

For information about the Bronco Raptor’s crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

Ford offers competitive limited and powertrain warranties. However, the company doesn’t provide complimentary scheduled maintenance, whereas Jeep does.

#4406. Scout's New Factory Is Already Making Trucks. But You Won't Be Able To Buy One For A While

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Scout's new South Carolina factory has started producing vehicles, the company announced Thursday. They're not production cars, and they're not for sale, but it's a big step on the company's path to market.

The factory is now building validation vehicles that will be used for further development. That means they'll be undergoing real-world testing and refinement, and be used to iterate the production process and final vehicle design.

The company has about a year to learn those lessons before it is supposed to start producing final, sellable models. It has said that production of sellable vehicles will begin next year, with first deliveries set for 2028. In a world where so many EVs have been delayed or canceled, too, the company is publicly signaling its intent to deliver.

That doesn't mean it's been an easy road. The company's "Harvester" extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) have proven far more popular among pre-orderers than the company expected, with the vast majority of reservation holders skipping the purely electric option. That's why the range-extended Traveler SUV will launch first, followed by the Terra pickup and pure-electric models. Like most automakers, the company seems to have overestimated demand for the pure electric models when it was initially announced.

The entire segment has largely been creamed. The two most popular all-electric truck models—the Ford F-150 Lightning and Tesla Cybertruck—have both been canceled as of last week. Buyers have proven unwilling to pay a large premium for purely electric trucks. That's why Ram killed its all-electric truck program in favor of an upcoming EREV truck, why the next Lightning will get a range extender, and why Scout is focusing on the Harvester models.

But that market is also unproven. Ram's EREV has been delayed a number of times, and the Scout and Ford remain a ways off. The question is whether EREVs can overcome the pricing challenges that electric trucks have faced without compromising on utility or range. Given that all of these brands are planning to over over 500 miles of range on a full battery and a full tank, I don't expect usability issues. Until we see detailed pricing, though, it's hard to know how big of a market this will be.

Regardless, Scout has a lot of advantages. It has the backing of Volkswagen, an automotive giant. It will benefit from that company's tie-up with Rivian, which should lead to excellent software and lower production costs. And it's using a great name in a real niche: proper off-road, solid-axle trucks and SUVs. Add in a bench seat and a great design and you certainly have my interest.

But as we've seen time and time again, actually launching a new brand is tough. The company has to navigate a flurry of dealer lawsuits and a challenging automotive environment, all while sustaining our interest for another year. It's far from a guaranteed success. But today, Scout got a bit closer to the finish line.

#4404. Jeep Just Got into the Retro-Gaming Groove with ‘Moab Run’

The game lets you play as one of seven special-edition Jeeps on Utah's Sand Flats Road.

Modern driving games like Snowrunner or Gran Turismo harness massive computing power to accurately model the physics of piloting a vehicle at speed. Sometimes, however, you just want an overexcited announcer to shout “Awesome!” while you sail a Jeep Gladiator over a crest, misjudge the landing, and impact an immovable sandstone massif at 85 mph.

Such is the appeal of Moab Run, a new retro-themed off-roading game from none other than Jeep itself. Playable on mobile or in a browser window, the game channels the best of 1990s-era 3-D games like Sega Rally or Offroad Challenge, infusing it with playable examples of the very real special-edition Wranglers Jeep has launched over the past year or so.

See all results for new 2027 Jeep Wrangler for sale near 98837

At launch, you can play seven of these Wranglers, from the synthwave-look Rewind to the military cosplay Sarge, with the full dozen coming to future game expansions. There’s also currently just the one course set in Utah at present, but two other tracks will become playable in due course.

Controls are very basic: accelerate, brake, and steer, with an option to powerslide and build up boost for bigger jumps. Jeep includes a somewhat hilarious disclaimer up front: “Do not attempt to recreate these actions in real life,” because, again, 85 mph into sandstone is not so fun in the non-digital world.

As befits a company that’s all about off-roading, the roads in Moab Run are basically just a guideline. You can switch between various overlapping routes, climb sandstone ridges to pick up collectible star points, or just ignore things completely and fly off the road into a canyon river. There are also hidden collectible ducks scattered across the map, because of course there are. It’s a Jeep Thing.

You can’t damage the Wranglers, you seemingly can’t get stuck, and if you purposely drive in the wrong direction, all that’ll happen is a large green arrow will appear to point to where you’re supposed to go. It’s basically a penalty-free way to blow off some steam, and the opposite of what technical real-world off-roading is like.

Also, it’s free. If you fancy getting in a little Jeep Wranglin’ action during your coffee break, Moab Run will do the trick. Go hunt down those hidden ducks, and aim for the hangtime challenge award.

#4403. America's Top 3 SUVs Are About To Be Hybrid Or Electric

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Recent moves from Toyota and Honda prove it once and for all: Pure gasoline options just can't hang with electrified power anymore. On Thursday, Honda announced that its best-selling CR-V crossover will be available exclusively as a hybrid starting with a redesigned 2028 model.

"With a 100% hybrid powertrain, the next-generation Honda CR-V will further expand the appeal of America's most popular SUV as demand for hybrid-electric vehicles reaches record levels," said Luis Guerra, assistant vice president of Honda National Auto Sales.

Arriving next year, the 2028 CR-V will kick off a seventh generation for the SUV and be powered exclusively by a new two-motor hybrid system. Honda says the tech will boost driving efficiency and expand the range where the engine operates most efficiently, as compared with its current hybrid system. Today, the CR-V is available with both hybrid and pure-combustion powertrains.

Toyota made the RAV4 exclusively a hybrid starting with the 2026 model. Now Honda is following suit.

The Honda news follows similar decisions by Toyota, which made the RAV4 SUV hybrid-only starting with the 2026 model. (The Camry, too, is now only a hybrid.)

Taken together, it means that soon the top three models in the heart of the U.S. car market will come with some form of electrification. That alone will do a lot for getting people into more efficient cars—even if they aren't ready for an EV yet. In 2025, the RAV4, CR-V, and Tesla Model Y were America's best-selling SUVs, responsible for some 1.2 million sales combined.

The move should give a further boost to hybrid sales in America, which have already been on a tear. In the third quarter, hybrids reached 16% of the U.S. light-duty vehicle market. Chalk it up to growing awareness, higher gas prices, and more options in the marketplace.

Those options are poised to grow even further as more automakers capitalize on growing interest in hybrids—particularly in the SUV segment. Nissan is readying a Rogue Hybrid with a unique hybrid system that makes it drive a lot like an EV. GM is reportedly bringing hybrid powertrains to its three-row SUVs, like the Chevy Traverse and GMC Acadia.

In a sense, it's a wonder the hybrid boom didn't happen sooner. Getting a hybrid instead of a gas vehicle is essentially a no-brainer. You may pay a little more up front, but research shows that the fuel savings over time pay off the difference fairly quickly. According to Consumer Reports, the average hybrid commands a $1,700 premium, but most models pay for themselves within four years.

Just remember: Full EVs are still the cheapest vehicles to run per mile, if you have home charging. They'll always be better for the environment than hybrids too. And the smooth, quiet driving experience is tough to beat. More hybrid Hondas are a step in the right direction, but with the automaker bowing out of the EV game for now, buyers looking to ditch gas entirely will have to look elsewhere.

#4402. Jensen Huang’s Departure from NVIDIA Sparks Hope of a Gaming Pivot

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

NVIDIA has announced that co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO whilst continuing as CFO, with Harvey Jones becoming the board’s first-ever chair. The announcement didn’t give a reason, although it obviously arrived after very public reports of extramarital affairs, one of them reportedly with a woman US intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. Neither NVIDIA nor Huang has confirmed the reporting, but investors reacted regardless, with shares falling as much as 14% at the open.

Masato Kumzawa addresses fan reactions to Grace Ashcroft's design and the impact of NVIDIA's DLSS 5 AI technology.

Ultimately, I’m not that interested in the gossip. What interests me far more is what happens to a company that has spent the last few years being defined by one man’s bet on AI, and whether that opens the door for the side of the business that first made NVIDIA a household name. For anyone who has tried to buy a graphics card recently, that is a rather important question.

Huang co-founded NVIDIA in 1993 and ran it for more than 33 years, with the move into AI being very much his decision. It has paid off enormously, because data centres now make up roughly 91.5% of the company’s revenue. The flip side is that nobody else has been quite as closely tied to that strategy, which makes for some interesting possibilities for NVIDIA’s future.

Kress has been CFO since 2013 and is a well-respected voice with the market, and eToro’s Josh Gilbert described her as a familiar and trusted presence, whilst adding that a company known for its technical edge might want an engineer in the chair. Analyst Dan Ives expects her stint as interim CEO to last around a year before NVIDIA looks outside. NVIDIA’s company structure is interesting in that it doesn’t make finding a solution any easier: Huang had more than 60 people reporting to him directly.

NVIDIA has no COO, and reports suggest there was no succession plan in place. The internal names analysts have put forward, such as Ian Buck, Bill Dally, Michael Kagan and Bryan Catanzaro, are largely AI and data centre figures, but none of them has been the face of the strategy in the way Huang was. Constellation Research’s Ray Wang pointed out that many of NVIDIA’s partnerships and investments came about because people trusted Jensen.

Which brings me to the hopium. NVIDIA started out making graphics cards for gamers, and CNBC has pointed out that those gamers helped keep the company afloat back in 1999 by buying the GeForce 256. These days they account for under 10% of revenue, and it shows: RTX 50-series production was reportedly cut by up to 40% earlier this year, the Super refresh was reportedly shelved, and the next generation has reportedly drifted towards 2028. Meanwhile, the RTX 5090 launched at $1,999 and third-party sellers have been asking far more than that ever since.

Nvidia DLSS 5 is officially supported in 2K27, but eager fans have found their own way to enable the software in a myriad of titles.

So it isn’t hard to see why some gamers are hoping the board promotes someone with roots on that side of the business. Jeff Fisher, SVP of GeForce, has been at NVIDIA since 1994, but it is obvious that Kress is probably the safer bet for investors. Jonah Alben, who has led GPU engineering since 2008, and co-founder Chris Malachowsky might also throw a hat into this race. It is however important to note that all of this is still very much speculation: nobody at NVIDIA has hinted at a gaming pivot, and whether that will happen with any likeliness will be heavily dependent on other factors.

Truth be told, I wouldn’t expect a new CEO to change much straight away, even one with a soft spot for gaming. The memory shortage squeezing GeForce is affecting the entire industry, with Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron reportedly prioritising AI customers for their high-bandwidth memory, and that won’t disappear because of who is sitting in the corner office.

Whoever takes over will also inherit a company that has just lost its founder and a fair amount of investor confidence, which tends to make boards cautious rather than adventurous. Even so, I’d quite like to see someone in charge who remembers where GeForce came from, and who has some sympathy for the people still trying to buy one. For now, Kress is running both the company and its finances whilst the search for a permanent CEO gets under way.

Between GTA 6's leaked pricing and the Steam Machine's $1,049 reveal, this week made one thing clear: gaming is getting expensive everywhere at once.

#4401. Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on the SSP

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.

As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer said in the memo reviewed by Reuters. The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer announced earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.

According to Autocar, Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.

Production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.

BMW has the new i3, and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.

Volkswagen said in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.

The company also said investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”

Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.

To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.

In March, VW said several test vehicles, including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.

However, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.

Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.

The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.

While development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

#4400. Tesla Just Culled the Cybertruck Lineup to a Single $112K Model

If you’re looking to order Tesla’s electric truck before it goes away for good, you’ll be limited to the tri-motor Cyberbeast.

Time is running out for the Tesla Cybertruck. Just last week, CEO Elon Musk announced that the company is winding down production of the polarizing electric pickup, which will officially go offline sometime in the middle of next year. While that might’ve set off alarm bells for anyone who is still hoping to order a new Cybertruck, there’s yet another twist to consider, and that’s the fact that Tesla has trimmed the lineup to a single model—and it’s the most expensive one.

If you head on over to Tesla’s consumer site and navigate to the Cybertruck’s ordering page, you’ll see that the Dual Motor All-Wheel Drive and Premium All-Wheel Drive models are no longer available to order. That leaves only the Cyberbeast, which has a starting price of $112,235 when you include the $250 non-refundable order fee and mandatory $1995 destination charge. Selecting additional options can push the truck’s price past $120K.

See all results for new 2027 Tesla Cybertruck for sale near 94133

As Not a Tesla App first pointed out, the Cyberbeast’s base price has risen by $10,000 since the start of the year, including $7500 since last week. Regardless of the price hikes, a $100,000 vehicle is still out of reach for most people, and that’s also likely the case for the now-discontinued Dual Motor AWD variant, which last started at nearly $85K with all the mandatory fees. Of course, even casual observers will agree that Tesla’s decision to trim the Cybertruck lineup to the single most expensive model is a way to maximize profits during the waning months of its life.

For those who can afford a new Cyberbeast, its hefty price tag brings impressive acceleration numbers, with the last version we tested hitting 60 mph in just 2.6 seconds (matching Tesla’s claim). However, the 834-hp tri-motor electric truck didn’t meet its 320-mile range estimate, with its battery running out of juice after 250 miles in our 75-mph real-world highway test. Pro tip: Keeping the Cybertruck’s roll-top bed cover closed saved us 25 miles of range at sustained highway speeds.

These are a few of the things we’ll have to remember it by. And if you’re feeling bummed that you can’t afford the last batch of new Cybertrucks, just remember that there are pre-owned models aplenty.

#4399. Slate Is Selling A $30 'Screenless GPS' For Its Low-Tech Truck

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Slate has introduced a new "Screenless GPS" for its bare-bones EV pickup. It has zero boot time, no subscription fees, unlimited battery life, and absolutely zero chance of telling you to make a left turn into an active construction site since it, well, doesn't actually do turn-by-turn directions.

If you haven't caught on yet, it's a book: Rand McNally's 2027 Road Atlas, to be precise. On Thursday, Slate added the map to its online store for $30, calling it "the original navigation system." Slate said it's available in limited quantities.

The new product is clearly tongue-in-cheek and a bit of a stunt, but it also speaks to what Slate is trying to pull off. The startup is betting that people are fed up enough with complicated, modern cars to embrace a no-frills EV with unpainted composite body panels, manual windows, and no big infotainment screen. That, of course, means no built-in navigation either.

Obviously, few drivers actually want to use a physical map these days. Fortunately, the Slate will come with a phone mount, so owners can continue using their favorite mapping apps, like Google or Apple Maps. And hey, maybe that Slate-branded Atlas could come in handy in a pinch.

"When it comes to tech, we believe you should use the devices and solutions you already know and love," Slate said Thursday. "Not because we don't like tech, but because we believe you already have everything you need to get where you're going."

That minimalist mentality is what has kept the battery-powered truck under $25,000. You get an LFP battery, a bed, some wheels, and freedom from the complexities of the modern automobile. And if you really do want to add on some extras, they can be as analog as a map, or as digital as your phone. Or as involved as an SUV kit with extra seats and a roof.

It's a bold bet in an era when cars seem to only be getting more expensive and more packed with screens. We won't have to wait too long to see if the gamble pays off. Slate plans to deliver its first trucks later this year.

#4397. A Record Number Of Uber Miles Are Happening In EVs

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Uber’s electrification efforts are looking better with every quarter, and this year’s third quarter has shown that the giant ride-hailing company is serious about lowering its fleet’s emissions. That said, Uber is also aware that, based on current trends, its 2030 goals “continue to be out of reach.”

Let’s focus on the good news first. Last quarter, Uber drivers across the globe completed a whopping 207.4 million rides in EVs, which boils down to over 26 EV trips on the ride-hailing platform every second, on average. Compared to the same period last year, the number of EV trips on the platform is 52% higher, but the big stats don’t end here.

In Europe, one in five Uber trips were done in an EV, while one in ten Americans and Canadians who took an Uber in Q3 wound up in an electric car. On average, there were 434,000 EV drivers active on Uber from July through September globally, up 52% from the same period last year,

When looking at the charts provided by the ride-hailing company, the difference between Europe and the U.S. and Canada is astonishing. Even from the start of the chart, in Q1 2021, Europe had a consistent lead when it comes to electrification, but the two North American countries were left in the dust starting in the third quarter of 2024. European drivers flocked to EVs, helped by various incentives and a boost in the charging infrastructure, while Americans' and Canadians’ uptake stayed relatively flat. For its part, Uber has offered cash bonuses to drivers who wanted to switch to an EV.

Despite the upward trends seen in the charts provided by Uber, it’s not all good news. The company has missed almost all of its sustainability targets for 2025 and is well on its way to missing its goals for the end of 2030 by a wide margin.

Just as the number of EVs on the ride-hailing platform has increased, plenty of drivers chose gas- or diesel-powered cars to make an extra buck on Uber. In the U.S. and Canada, every mile that a passenger traveled on Uber resulted in an average generation of 318 grams of carbon dioxide. That’s better than 2024’s 340 grams, but worse than the 306-gram average in 2023.

A similar story can be found in Europe, though the average vehicle emissions caused by Uber trips are vastly smaller than in the U.S. and Canada. Last year, 186 g of CO2 were put into the atmosphere in Europe for every mile traveled by a passenger on Uber. The figure is lower than in 2024 and 2023, but higher than the 183 g average in 2022.

The company said that the large gap between Europe and the U.S. and Canada can be linked to two factors. First, European drivers prefer EVs and hybrids more than American and Canadian drivers, but the more stringent fuel economy reporting standards in the U.S. also contribute to this discrepancy.

In 2025, the ride-hailing giant had wanted to see 100% of rides in London and Amsterdam be zero-emission. The outcome was just 41%. Furthermore, 50% of all mobility miles in seven European capitals were envisioned as being completed in electric vehicles, but the year ended with just 32%.

By the end of the decade, 100% of rides in Canada, Europe, and the U.S. should be zero-emission, but Uber is realistic and knows that it’s highly unlikely that it will finish 2030 with these numbers. Still, the company says it’s “deeply committed to this transition,” even though many levers are outside of its control.

#4395. Tesla Just Killed Its Cheapest All-Wheel-Drive Model Y

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Getting an all-wheel-drive Tesla Model Y just got a lot more expensive after the American company removed the entry-level version of the crossover from its online configurator.

The Model Y All-Wheel Drive, which used to cost roughly $42,000, is nowhere to be found on the automaker’s website, which means the most affordable dual-motor Model Y is now the Premium AWD trim that starts at $51,630.

Introduced in February, the now-defunct Model Y AWD came hot on the heels of the budget-oriented Model 3 Standard and Model Y Standard that debuted in October 2025 as more affordable, rear-wheel-drive-only versions of the company’s best-selling EVs. When the bare-bones Model Y AWD was introduced, Tesla also dropped the “Standard” badge from its lineup, though the other trims are still called “Premium” and “Performance”.

Powered by the same battery as the single-motor Model Y RWD, the discontinued Model Y AWD had the shortest claimed range in the Model Y lineup, with an EPA-estimated 294 miles on a full charge—54 miles less than the most affordable rear-driven crossover in Tesla’s lineup currently.

With two electric motors providing motivation, the dropped Model Y AWD could sprint from zero to 60 miles per hour in 4.6 seconds, 2.2 seconds faster than its single-motor counterpart, despite weighing roughly 200 pounds more.

The cheapest Model Y in Tesla’s lineup remains the basic RWD version, which starts at $41,630. Compared to the better-equipped and more expensive trims, the entry-level crossover comes with redesigned front and rear lights, passive shock absorbers, a lower 225-kilowatt maximum charging power, fewer speakers for the audio system, and seats trimmed in vegan leather and cloth. There’s no FM radio, no rear screen, no ventilated seats, and only the front seats are heated. Furthermore, while the glass roof is still installed, the base trim has a headliner that covers it entirely.

The discontinuation of the Tesla Model Y All-Wheel Drive is just the latest casualty in the company’s quest to slim down its passenger-vehicle lineup. Earlier this year, the Model S and Model X were axed, and their production line has been ripped out of the factory to make room for robots. More recently, Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced that the Cybertruck would be retired next year. Until that happens, the only trim remaining is the top Cyberbeast, which starts at $109,990.

There are no plans to replace the Model S and Model X, and the Cybercab two-seater will take over the Cybertruck’s floor space.

#4394. Tested: The 2026 Lexus ES Hybrid Evolves, but It Has a Familiar Feel

Larger than before and with a significantly revamped interior, the new ES350h nonetheless stays the course with its cushy driving demeanor.

11/12/26 UPDATE: This review has been updated with instrumented test results.

Although Lexus is no stranger to sporty models, this luxury brand made its name on quiet, plush sedans that prioritize refinement above all else. And the ES is the one that has persisted. This comfy cruiser was the bestselling Lexus for many years, and it continues to attract a loyal set of buyers. Understandably, Lexus has been reluctant to change the ES formula much throughout its seven generations thus far.

On the surface, that appears to change with the new eighth-generation Lexus ES. Not only does the ES look quite different inside and out for 2026, but it also offers an electric powertrain for the first time. The ES hybrid continues, however, and after driving the latest version, it’s clear that this sedan's core mission hasn't changed as much as you might think.

Lexus first offered the ES as a hybrid for 2013, and the previous-generation gas-electric model made up around 40 percent of ES sales last year. Given that take rate, it makes sense that the old nonhybrid V-6 has been axed. The electric ES, which we review separately, is a big departure for this model line, but Lexus expects the hybrid to make up 80 percent of ES sales in the U.S. So, for now at least, the EV will be a niche product, and the gas-electric model will be the volume seller.

See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 34951

With a longer wheelbase, a significantly taller profile, and a more imposing shape, the new ES stretches to the larger end of the mid-size luxury-sedan segment. Lexus engineers say they tried to “eliminate the negatives” of the sedan shape with this model, such as the more difficult ingress and egress of a lower seating height. In other words, it follows the tall-sedan format of the Toyota Crown but attempts to disguise its stature with more angular styling and a swoopy roofline that tapers toward the short trunk lid. There are some awkward angles, but overall, the design works and is still recognizable as a Lexus.

The ES hybrid gets the latest Toyota hybrid powertrain, which the company refers to as the sixth-generation setup. It has a different power unit and transmission than before, and it’s configured to prioritize the electric motors for propulsion more. The 2.5-liter gasoline four-cylinder engine doesn’t change much, but total combined output of 244 horsepower is up from the previous ES300h’s 215 horses. That’s apparently enough for Lexus to bump the badge up to ES350h. All-wheel drive is optional on the hybrid ES for the first time, courtesy of an additional electric motor on the rear axle, though it doesn’t change output figures compared with the front-wheel-drive configuration.

The all-wheel-drive ES350h we tested got to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, which is a significant improvement over the previous, front-wheel-drive ES300h F Sport’s 7.9-second run. That’s despite a significant weight gain, as our test car tipped the scales at 4145 pounds, 352 more than the 2023 ES300h we last tested.

See all results for new 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 34951

While this four-cylinder powertrain isn’t quite as smooth or sonorous as the old nonhybrid ES350’s V-6, the upgraded gas-electric setup is appreciably more refined than the old hybrid was. The gas engine is well isolated from the cabin and only makes itself known under hard acceleration; the hushed 67 decibels and 21 sones of noise we recorded inside at 70 mph is perfectly acceptable here. The electric motors go about their business seamlessly, with imperceptible switching between gas and electric power, and while the embiggened ES doesn’t quite feel eager, it accelerates with sufficient gusto and generally is responsive to throttle inputs. EPA ratings sit at 46 mpg combined with front-wheel drive and 44 mpg with all-wheel drive—strong numbers for this large of a sedan. We averaged 37 mpg overall, and the ES matched its 42-mpg EPA highway estimate in our 75-mph real-world fuel-economy test. But that’s not quite as good as the previous model, a 2019 ES300h which managed 45 mpg in the same test.

Importantly, the ride quality is fantastic. The suspension is tuned to be soft, as you’d expect for a boulevardier like this, but we appreciate the nicely controlled body motions. And the all-season tires have plenty of sidewall for soaking up potholes and rough sections of road (relatively small 19-inch wheels are the only choice on the hybrid model for now). This isn’t a vehicle for hard cornering, and the eco-conscious rubber doesn’t provide much grip when you push it around corners, but the steering wheel feels good in your hands and provides satisfactory on-center feel and natural effort buildup. We recorded a ho-hum 0.84 g of grip around our skidpad and a 170-foot stop from 70 mph.

Upon first glance at the cabin, you might worry that Lexus has too eagerly adopted the button-free, touch-capacitive interiors that are becoming too commonplace. And while there are definitely fewer buttons and knobs than before, and more controls integrated into the large 14.0-inch touchscreen, Lexus has done a good job balancing function with form. There’s still a volume knob, for instance, and although most climate functions are now on a lower part of the screen, there are a few crucial tactile buttons for adjusting the temperature and turning on the defrosters. The steering-wheel controls look like they’re touch-sensitive, but they’re thankfully tactile too. And the secondary functions such as mirror controls, seat adjustments, and windows are all still conventional and intuitive.

The material finishes and build quality live up to Lexus’s high standard. But it is worth noting that the hybrid comes in Premium and Premium+ trims, which means it doesn’t offer some of the most high-end features and accoutrements of the electric model’s Luxury trim. Pricing for the ES350h ($51,095 to start) is up $6380 over the previous ES300h, but you do get more car—namely in the physical sense—and the ES still costs significantly less than a BMW 5-series or a Mercedes-Benz E-class. Our Premium-trim test car featured a few options and still came in at under $55,000.

Lexus is notoriously risk-averse with its most popular models, and ultimately the company’s conservatism has paid off with this new ES. It’s more modern-looking inside and out and offers more technology than before, but Lexus wisely didn’t make many changes to the core tenets that have made the ES a success. It still offers a comfortable ride and a cosseting interior, and these qualities combined with the hybrid powertrain’s quiet operation and impressive fuel efficiency should continue to please the ES faithful.

#4393. 10 Ocarina of Time Remake Changes That Break the Hearts of Nostalgic Fans

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

The remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has brought one of the most beloved and iconic adventures in gaming history back to life with a revamped visual presentation, plenty of gameplay improvements, and a surprising number of small changes that make exploring Hyrule feel fresh all over again. From quality-of-life improvements to the inventory and equipment systems to subtle environmental tweaks, there's literally a lot to appreciate about Nintendo's new take on this timeless classic.

However, as someone who grew up playing the original (and has an admittedly unhealthy amount of nostalgia running through my veins), I couldn't help but notice that some of the little things I loved are no longer around – or they are, but in a very different way.

Thomas Mahler believes Nintendo missed an opportunity to improve the level design in the Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake.

Don't get me wrong, I absolutely adore this remake and described it as a lovely modern remake with an old soul, but that doesn't mean I'm not allowed to miss a few things from my childhood, right? So, please allow me to put my nostalgic glasses on for a moment and revisit ten changes that have left a tiny hole in my heart.

One of my favorite things about the original Ocarina of Time was starting a new save file and giving Link the most ridiculous name I could think of. It was such a simple feature, but it opened the door to some quite hilarious moments, especially when characters started addressing the legendary hero using whatever silly name I'd come up with.

One of my personal favorites was naming him “Bro.” Suddenly, every conversation in Hyrule sounded like everyone was part of the most laid-back adventure imaginable.

Unfortunately, the remake has decided to put an end to our creative freedom by locking the protagonist's name to Link. I can understand the reasoning, especially considering Nintendo's efforts to make the franchise more accessible to new generations and expand its presence across other media (since the live-action movie is coming hot). Still, I'll always miss my little adventures with Bro. You will be missed, buddy.

One of the coolest easter eggs in the original Ocarina of Time was hidden in the courtyard where you first meet Princess Zelda. As Child Link, you must sneak past the castle guards to reach the princess without getting caught. Once you've had your little chat with her, however, there's nothing stopping you from exploring the area and discovering a few fun secrets.

Among them is a window you can shoot with your Slingshot, prompting a particularly grumpy guard to throw a bomb in your direction (how rude!). But that's not all. If you look through the other windows, you'll find three familiar faces from the Super Mario universe: Mario, Luigi, and Bowser, all sporting their Super Mario 64 appearances.

I was honestly expecting Nintendo to bring this little crossover back using the characters' more modern designs, perhaps even their Super Mario Odyssey models. Instead, the entire reference has been removed from the remake. It's a shame, considering how charming these little Nintendo Easter eggs can be. At least the guard is still there to throw a bomb at your face. Some traditions must be preserved, I suppose.

If there's one thing every Ocarina of Time veteran knows, it's that Rupees are important, and there's no shame in taking advantage of a good farming opportunity. One of the earliest places where you could stock up on some extra cash was a room inside Hyrule Castle's Market, conveniently filled with breakable pots.

As Child Link, you could simply walk inside, smash everything in sight, collect the Rupees, leave, and come back to find the pots replenished. Rinse and repeat until your pockets were sufficiently full.

Unfortunately, the remake has decided that we shouldn't be allowed to get rich quite so easily. While you can still find some pots containing Rupees in the room, they no longer respawn simply by leaving the castle and coming back inside. Instead, you'll have to wait quite a while and spend some time doing other activities before they return. I guess we'll just have to go back to cutting grass like the rest of Hyrule's hardworking citizens.

I know what you're thinking – why on earth would anyone miss Kaepora Gaebora being annoying? But hear me out, I promise there's a reason behind my questionable opinion!

I also ain't a fan of the original owl. In fact, I probably spent more time than I'd like to admit accidentally answering “No” when he asked whether I wanted to hear his explanation again. And if you've played the original, you know exactly how frustrating that could be. However, there was something strangely entertaining about collectively hating this overly talkative bird. Kaepora became one of those characters that practically every Ocarina of Time player had a story about, and that shared frustration was part of the experience.

Now, the remake has given him a much cuter appearance, and he's also significantly less annoying, behaving much more like the wise and mysterious owl he's supposed to be. I mean, where’s the fun in that? I can't help missing the days when simply seeing him fly toward me filled me with dread.

Ocarina of Time has plenty of memorable exploit tricks, but one of my personal favorites involved getting a Heart Piece much earlier than Nintendo originally intended.

In the original game, you could perform a particularly well-timed backflip from the top of Death Mountain, near the entrance to Goron City, and land on the roof of Dodongo's Cavern. This allowed you to grab a Heart Piece that was normally intended for Adult Link, long before you were supposed to have access to it. It was just one of those silly little tricks that made exploring Hyrule feel even more rewarding.

Well, those days are over. The remake has adjusted the backflip's height, making it considerably less effective, and even tweaked the position of Dodongo's Cavern entrance to prevent players from pulling off the same trick (not that I tried to do it or anything).

From suspicious house designs to familiar songs, fans think they've found clues.

There's an unwritten rule among players: the moment you unlock the Hookshot, you must immediately equip it and start shooting at everything in sight. And one of your first destinations will probably be the rooftops of Kakariko Village.

This was really fun because it offered more freedom than simply using it to reach the obvious targets. You could experiment with different surfaces, discover unexpected ways to navigate the environment, and generally mess around with an incredibly useful piece of equipment. Apparently, however, that wasn't quite what Nintendo had in mind. The remake has restricted the Hookshot's functionality, meaning it can now only latch onto specific designated targets, such as stone markers and certain treasure chests.

I understand that this might have been done to prevent unintended shortcuts or make progression more controlled, but I can't help feeling that something has been lost in the process. One of the most enjoyable aspects of Ocarina of Time was experimenting with your equipment and discovering creative ways to use it. So, please, Nintendo, give us our old Hookshot back!

One of my most vivid childhood memories of Ocarina of Time involves something that probably sounds completely ridiculous to anyone who didn't grow up playing the original: stepping into Hyrule Field for the very first time and desperately running toward Hyrule Castle like a lunatic.

That happened because, if night fell before we reached the castle gates, they would close, leaving Link stranded outside until morning – and Hyrule Field at night was not exactly the safest place to be.

And you’ve guessed: the remake has removed this particular inconvenience, meaning you no longer have to worry about being locked out of Hyrule Castle after sunset. My adult self appreciates not having to deal with that little problem, but the child in me misses those frantic nighttime sprints.

There's something wonderfully weird about the little laboratory at Lake Hylia. Inside, you'll find a rather eccentric scientist who spends most of his time complaining about his back pain while standing next to a water tank.

He'll even offer you a reward if you manage to dive deep enough to touch the bottom of the pool. Naturally, being the helpful hero that you are, you'll want to give it a try. But once you reach the bottom, you'll discover something rather unexpected: a shark inside a cage.

What made this little discovery even funnier in the original game was the shark itself! Rather than featuring a detailed 3D model, it was represented by a hilariously low-resolution, static image. It looked so out of place that it became one of those bizarre little details you simply couldn't forget. While the remake has kept the shark in the aquarium, unfortunately, it has also given it a proper visual upgrade. Sure, it looks considerably better now, but I miss the ridiculous charm of that pixelated little creature.

If there's one thing Ocarina of Time does exceptionally well, it's turning a seemingly innocent adventure into a horror game without any warning! One moment you're exploring a dungeon and collecting treasures, and the next you're desperately running for your life from something that looks like it escaped from your worst nightmare.

Few enemies capture that feeling better than the Wallmaster, a giant disembodied hand that suddenly drops from the ceiling, grabs Link, and sends him all the way back to the beginning of the area or dungeon.

And what made this enemy so terrifying in the original was the anticipation. You couldn't simply look up to check whether it was coming, so you had to rely on an increasingly unsettling sound effect and the shadow that gradually appeared above Link. The remake preserves most of these elements, but introduces one rather important difference: a spotlight that illuminates the area whenever it’s about to appear. Combined with its shadow, this makes the enemy practically announce its arrival in the most dramatic way possible.

I appreciate the warning, but I honestly miss the uncertainty that made these encounters so frightening in the original. Thankfully, the Dead Hand is absolutely nightmare-inducing in the remake, so I'll let this one slide.

Remember the Water Temple? If you played the original Ocarina of Time back in the day, there's a good chance that simply reading those two words made you feel a little uncomfortable.

For years, this dungeon had a reputation for being one of the most frustrating experiences in the entire game. Between constantly changing the water level and switching between the Iron Boots and other equipment, it was enough to test even the most patient players.

There was also a particularly nasty Small Key hidden underneath the floor of the central pillar, which could only be accessed after raising the water level. It was incredibly easy to overlook, and if you ever found yourself seemingly stuck with no idea how to progress, there's a good chance this little key was the culprit!

Despite keeping most of the original dungeon's layout intact, the remake has made things considerably easier by removing this easily missed Small Key altogether. This means players no longer have to spend ages retracing their steps and wondering whether they've somehow managed to softlock their game.

Of course, the Water Temple is still a memorable dungeon, and I'm certainly not complaining about a more streamlined experience. But I do find it funny that an entire generation of players had to suffer through those confusing corridors just so newcomers could have a slightly more pleasant time! You're welcome, younger Zelda fans. We fought in the trenches so you wouldn't have to.

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

#4391. Audi A4 EV Delayed Amid VW Group Financial Troubles: Report

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Audi has delayed the introduction of the electric A4 sedan by roughly one year, according to Autocar, which quotes an inside source at the German automaker. The electric A4, which was supposed to go into production at the company’s main plant in Ingolstadt in 2028, will go head-to-head with the BMW i3 and Mercedes-Benz C-Class EVs, which are already available in Europe.

The delay is reportedly tied to the Volkswagen Group’s worsening financial situation, software woes linked to the long-delayed Scalable Systems Platform (SSP), and Audi’s desire to make significant changes to the underbody of what should have been a common design across SSP-based electric sedans.

The current-generation Audi A5, which replaced the A4, is available with a plug-in hybrid powertrain.

Autocar’s source said that the premium German automaker requested bespoke footwells for both front and rear passengers instead of the completely flat floor that many purpose-built EVs use today. The reason behind this big demand reportedly has to do with the brand’s desire to deliver the packaging, seating position, and interior proportions that have traditionally been offered by the A4.

What’s more, the BMW i3 rival will supposedly use a 48-volt electrical system for its accessories instead of the traditional 12V setup that had been planned originally. Just like in the Tesla Cybertruck, adopting a higher-voltage system enables the automaker to use thinner-gauge wire and install higher-powered computers.

However, the changes come at a tough time for Audi’s parent company, VW Group, which is ditching grandiose plans and doing everything it can to limit the cash bleeding. The upcoming Volkswagen ID. Golf, which is also based on the SSP architecture, has been delayed, leaving the marque with its current lineup of electric models until the end of the decade.

For what it’s worth, the VW Group’s new lineup of affordable EVs is doing very well in Europe, but the money problem persists. The company can’t make them fast enough to keep up with demand, but building gas cars is still more profitable. This conundrum has put the German auto industry giant in a tough spot, where it’s trying to keep factories alive, but the importance of the vehicles that are currently being assembled there is slowly fading.

The first SSP-based cars were originally planned for 2026, but so far, not a single production model has been assembled.

#4390. BYD’s new flagship Tang SUV starts at about $34,000 with two enormous screens

BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China. This five-seat flagship SUV packs more than you’d expect for the money, with two massive 30-inch-plus screens inside and up to 850 km (528 miles) of CLTC range.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the new model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD announced on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD said.

Like many of its new flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty division said third-gen Tang vehicles have arrived at dealerships nationwide.

Why mention "two enormous screens" like they are some markers of a more premium vehicle or represent some value? We don't measure the utility of cars by screen real estate per dollar. It's the other part of the utility that matter: range, driving dynamics, road trip convenience, fit/finish/materials/insulation. Personally, I don't think "enormous screens" are going to age well as an automotive trend.

The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it launched in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500) a CLTC driving range of 800 km (497 miles). Starting at just 269,900 yuan ($40,000), the Flagship EV version uses a bigger (130.15 kWh) battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 590 miles (950 km).

Will BYD’s smaller five-seat SUV draw the same demand? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

#4389. Scout’s New Truck and SUV Are Another Step Closer to Reality

The VW-owned company has started validation builds of the Terra and Traveler at its new $2 billion factory in Blythewood, South Carolina.

Just like vehicles themselves, automotive manufacturing plants have to go through a lot of testing before cranking out the first production model. Scout Motors broke ground on its Blythewood, South Carolina, plant about two and a half years ago, and as final bits of construction wrap up, the VW Group subsidiary is beginning to build validation vehicles to test production processes.

When Scout reemerged a few years ago to bring back the practical, can-do vehicles that defined the brand in the 1960s and ’70s, it aimed to build a fleet of hybrid and electric body-on-frame off-roaders that blended modern amenities with vintage charm. The automaker plans to launch a Terra pickup truck and a Traveler SUV for the 2028 model year.

See all results for new 2028 Scout Terra for sale near 90011

It looks like Scout is still on track to stick with that timeline. The automaker has announced that most of the manufacturing parts are already up and running, with validation vehicles beginning to make their way through the body, paint, and assembly shops. Validation vehicles are kind of like a practice run, giving employees the ability to problem-solve and refine processes without having to keep a tight schedule.

Alongside the new equipment, Scout is testing out more than 750 robots in the body shop. The AI-supported bots will be used to monitor about 5000 weld points per vehicle for quality assurance. At full capacity, the body shop will be able to process about 40 vehicles per hour.

The Terra pickup and Traveler SUV are both expected to start at under $60,000. Scout says the validation process will continue into 2027, followed by more refined pre-production vehicles and eventually the finalized production model. That’s right in line with what Scott Keogh, Scout’s CEO, told us last year, when he projected that the first vehicles would go on sale by the end of 2027. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2028.

#4388. The VW ID. Buzz Is Getting A New Job As A Robotaxi

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The Volkswagen ID. Buzz hasn't exactly been a smash hit in the U.S. But that hasn't stopped commercial customers from eyeing up the nostalgic electric van for something it's particularly good at: moving people.

May Mobility announced on Thursday that it plans to integrate its autonomous driving systems into the Buzz to give it a job wherever driverless taxis are welcome.

May wants to use its existing tech stack to equip up to the ID. Buzzes with hardware and software that can see "up to 10 seconds into the future."

Well, kind of—May's tech uses onboard predictive modeling to anticipate how the world around it will move, similar how a human assess other drivers around them. It creates multiple scenarios in its digital brain and uses the model's reasoning to determine which one is most suited for its environment.

The tech would also make the cars capable of integrating with any of the "global robotaxi platforms," which is one of the ways that May is approaching its partnership-first business model. Presumably, that means its existing fleet partners like Lyft, Uber, and other ride hailing services around the world.

May's approach is also a silent win for folks who want to make sure that Buzz doesn't fizzle out.

One of the biggest blockers to Buzz adoption on the consumer side has been the price. While that could change in the coming months, the van's initially high price tag and just so-so range made it a fairly lukewarm offering to EV buyers looking to park the Buzz in their own driveway. That's why Robotaxis might be the best use of the Buzz yet.

It's roomy enough to comfortably haul plenty of passengers (and whatever cargo they bring along), plus it has the easy ingress and egress of a minivan. Other companies seem to agree, even VW's own MOIA arm that recently began testing an autonomous version of the Buzz in Los Angeles.

So far, May has completed about 600,000 commercial driverless rides in the U.S. and Japan. And while it hasn't said how many cars it operates, May is pretty open about its long-term goal for the Buzz.

It plans to put 10,000 of these autonomous ID. Buzzes on the road by 2031. That all starts with road testing early next year, followed by delivering the first fleet vehicles to customers by 2028.

#4387. Volkswagen may have just hinted at the name of its next affordable EV

Volkswagen is getting ready to launch a new electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW plans to call it.

The new entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

The new model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

Volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its new MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

Volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

Volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

The VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a new 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine new models VW plans to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen previously said the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

Volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

In March, the Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies (RV Tech) joint venture tested the new SDV architecture on the ID. EVERY1, alongside Audi and Scout reference vehicles, validating over-the-air (OTA) capabilities.

The new architecture will enable “highly automated driving features” and “advanced infotainment solutions,” with continuous OTA updates.

While VW said it will deploy the SDV architecture in “electric vehicles across markets in the Western Hemisphere,” the entry-level EV is not expected to reach the States.

Volkswagen is, however, preparing to launch the ID. Tiguan, which will launch in 2027 as the successor to the ID.4 (and ID.5 in Europe).

#4386. 2027 McLaren W1

They say that lightning never strikes the same place twice, let alone thrice, but McLaren is channeling Zeus with its newest W1 flagship. As a descendant of the hallowed McLaren F1 and a direct successor to the brand's last 903-hp P1 halo car, the W1 assumes a throne previously occupied by hypercar royalty. And if you couldn’t guess by its wind-sculpted, carbon-fiber-laden exterior, the W1 has the spec sheet to back up its noble position.

Wielding a 9200-rpm twin-turbo V-8 paired with an axial-flux electric motor, the W1 delivers 1258 horsepower to the pavement via its rear wheels, making it the most powerful McLaren ever. Those ponies don’t have to contend with much mass, as a carbon-fiber tub and body help keep the W1's dry weight to a feathery 3084 pounds. Active aerodynamics, including a rear wing that extends rearward up to 11.8 inches, add massive downforce and enable maximum attack at the racetrack. The W1 is a worthy heir to its predecessors, the latest in a highly accomplished bloodline of supersonic, roadgoing weaponry.

Expert Tip: When it comes to seven-digit, Formula-1-inspired race cars for the road, options are predictably limited. The Aston Martin Valhalla is another example, brandishing a 1064-horsepower plug-in-hybrid powertrain and a chassis developed with help from the Aston Martin Aramco Formula 1 Team.

With the W1 debuting just last year, we don’t expect any changes for the 2027 model year.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

The W1 uses a plug-in hybrid powertrain comprised of McLaren's MHP-8 turbocharged V-8 engine working in unison with a radial-flux electric motor and an 8-speed transmission; it sends power to the rear wheels. The V-8 alone is good for 916 horsepower, and the electric motor 342 horsepower. Combined, that's 1258 ponies, the highest output of any McLaren.

The electric element includes a motorsport-derived E-module: a radial flux motor and integrated Motor Control Unit weighing just 44 pounds, similar to the type used in IndyCar racing. (McLaren participates in that series as well as F1.) The electric motor is mounted to the transmission and can spin up to 24,000 rpm. The E-module is powered by a battery of about 1.4 kWh, enclosed in a structural carbon-fiber box located low in the chassis to optimize the center of gravity. The battery maintains a minimum level of charge to crank the engine on vehicle start-up and to power the electric reversing function. McLaren quotes an electric-only driving range of about two miles and a charging time of 22 minutes to bring the battery to 80 percent.

#4385. Tesla Opens Self-Driving Cybercab Orders To 'Select Customers' At $29,990

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Tesla will soon start selling its steering wheel-free Cybercab for personal use, the company announced on Friday.

The Cybercab will cost $29,990, undercutting the Model 3 by $7,000 and making the golden two-seater Tesla's cheapest vehicle ever. According to a screenshot of the order page shared by Tesla, deliveries will begin as soon as next month.

There are a few catches. The Cybercab won't operate anywhere in the country, Tesla says, but rather in "supported service areas." It will also require a $299-per-month autonomous driving subscription to operate, with the first month included for no charge. That totals to some $3,600 per year just to use the vehicle, before insurance or maintenance costs.

And the model will be sold to hand-picked buyers, at least to start. "Select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use," the company said in a tweet on its Robotaxi X account. Tesla said initial availability is limited.

It's not clear when or if sales will expand to the general public. But the sale of a car one can actually own that is capable of driving itself without supervision would be a massive milestone for both the automotive world and for Tesla in particular.

Putting autonomous cars in the hands of regular people has been one of Elon Musk's central promises for about a decade, and he's missed his self-imposed deadlines year after year. Meanwhile, today's driverless cars are owned and operated by companies running ride-hailing services, like Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla—not by individuals. The Cybercabs in operation today are part of Tesla's Robotaxi service, which opened for business last year and now shuttles riders around in a handful of U.S. cities, including Austin and Miami.

Tesla's biggest boosters online cheered the news. But it's also sure to tick off some of the many Tesla owners who have paid for Full Self-Driving over the years and have been waiting patiently for their Model 3s and Model Ys to become autonomous. Most recently, Musk said that will happen in the second quarter of next year in areas where the Robotaxi service operates.

The Tesla Cybercab has two seats and no steering wheel or pedals.

Tesla is far from the only company looking to sell autonomous cars to the public someday. Rivian plans to introduce lidar and a new in-house chip to the R2 in the hopes of giving it self-driving capability someday. General Motors plans to introduce an eyes-off version of Super Cruise to the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. It'll operate on highways first before expanding to other road types, GM says.

Tesla advertises the personally-owned Cybercab as "fully autonomous" and says owners will be able to monitor their vehicles and manage rides via the Tesla app. But overall, the announcement raises almost as many questions as it answers.

For example, there was no mention of whether customers would be able to add their cabs to the Robotaxi fleet and earn passive income, another longtime Musk promise. It's also not clear where the Cybercab will be able to operate, nor whether Tesla will expand that territory quickly enough to make buying one worthwhile beyond a handful of cities.

Another cloud of uncertainty looming over the Cybercab's rollout is regulatory in nature. The Cybercab's unconventional design has caught the attention of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which questions how exactly Tesla determined that the vehicle complies with motor vehicle safety standards. The Tesla lacks a steering wheel, pedals, and side-view mirrors, all things that are typically required for a car to be street-legal.

The federal government lets companies apply to roll out noncompliant vehicles, but those deployments are capped at 2,500 vehicles per year. (Zoox, for its part, was recently granted an exemption to commercially deploy 5,000 of its autonomous pods over two years.) NHTSA has said it's working to streamline autonomous-vehicle rules, which could work in Tesla's favor here.

If Tesla can pull this off, it'll be one for the history books. Of course, the company has made numerous ambitious promises around self-driving cars—like 1 million robotaxis by 2020, and unsupervised self-driving pretty much every year since—and it has generally fallen short. Whether the Cybercab rollout breaks that streak is still to be determined.

#4384. Rinnai’s new heat pump water heaters get smarter – and easier to install

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

The lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

The new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai says the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.
